### B.2 BatchTopK Sparsity

For every SAE in this paper, sparsity is imposed using a BatchTopK mechanism in which a hidden state $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is first mapped to non-negative pre-activations

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{f}}=\mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}})+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{enc}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m},$
| | (5)

and only the largest pre-activations are retained across the batch.
For a batch $X=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}$ , the pre-activations $\{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}$ are flattened into a single vector of length $Bm$ , and the sparse activation $\mathbf{f}_{i}$ is obtained by keeping only the top $kB$ entries globally and setting all others to zero.
The reconstruction is then

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{f}_{i}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}.$
| | (6)

In practice, after training with exact BatchTopK selection, inference uses an equivalent thresholded form

| | $f_{ij}=\tilde{f}_{ij}\,\mathbf{1}[\tilde{f}_{ij}>\theta],$
| | (7)

where the threshold $\theta$ is estimated from training-time top- $k$ statistics.
The Persistent SAE uses the resulting sparse activation as its token-wise sparse activation $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ ; only its downstream use differs.

The batch-level budget interacts with the persistent state in a way that is worth making explicit. In a flat baseline, the batch consists of shuffled tokens from many documents, and the global top- $kB$ selection allocates activations across this mixture. In the Persistent SAE, the batch consists of contiguous sequences, so the selection allocates activations across positions within a small number of documents. The average number of active features per token is the same in both cases, but the distribution across positions may differ. Using the thresholded form at inference removes this dependence on batch composition and makes the token-wise activation a deterministic function of the current hidden state.

### B.3 Persistence Parameterisation

The timescale parameters of the Persistent SAE must be parameterised so that the requirements of Section 4 hold throughout training. Three considerations guide this choice.

Stability. 
The state update in Equation 2 is applied repeatedly over sequences of hundreds of tokens, so any parameterisation that allows the state to grow without bound would produce inputs to the decoder whose scale depends on position. This would both complicate optimisation and make reconstructions at late positions incomparable to those at early positions. We therefore constrain the timescale parameters to a range in which the update is contractive, and we normalise the contribution of new evidence so that the state remains on the same scale as the token-wise activations it integrates.

Avoiding degenerate timescales. 
A timescale that is effectively infinite would cause a feature to retain the first evidence it receives for the remainder of the sequence, which is undesirable both because it prevents the feature from responding to new context and because it creates ill-conditioned gradients through long chains of updates. We therefore impose a hard cap that keeps every feature’s effective memory finite. At the other extreme, a memoryless timescale is permitted, since it recovers standard SAE behaviour for that feature.

Optimisation. 
The timescale parameters are optimised jointly with the encoder and decoder. We use an unconstrained parameter for each feature, mapped through a squashing function to the admissible range, so that the optimiser does not need to handle explicit constraints. We initialise these parameters to an intermediate value, away from the saturated regions of the squashing function, so that gradients with respect to the timescales are not vanishingly small at the start of training and each feature’s timescale can move in either direction.

Together, these choices make the Persistent SAE a well-behaved extension of a BatchTopK SAE: at initialisation it differs from a standard SAE only by moderate smoothing of activations over time, and over training each feature’s timescale is free to move within a bounded range.

## Appendix C Dataset Details

We use three datasets for distinct parts of the evaluation. Pile documents provide the hidden states used to train and evaluate the SAEs, MMLU questions provide subject-labelled text for analysing the persistent state, and AgentDojo trajectories support the prompt-injection monitoring case study. We describe each dataset and our use of it below.

### C.1 Pile Corpus

The original Pile is an $825$  GiB English-language corpus assembled from 22 sources, including academic papers, web pages, books, code, and online discussions [22]. We use the Pile Uncopyrighted release [35], a derived version that removes the Books3, BookCorpus2, OpenSubtitles, YouTube Subtitles, and OpenWebText2 components. Documents are accessed in streaming mode and shuffled with a buffer of size $10{,}000$ using a fixed seed. A document is accepted if, after tokenisation with the model tokeniser and truncation to the context cap, it contains at least the required minimum number of tokens.

Each accepted document is passed through the model, and the chosen residual-stream hidden states are retained.
If a sequence has retained length $L$ , temporal statistics are computed on token positions $\{16,\dots,L-1\}$ after dropping the initial tokens. Dropping an initial prefix is a standard precaution: hidden states at the first few positions of a sequence are known to have atypical norms and statistics, and including them can distort averages computed over positions.

The diversity of the Pile is relevant to any analysis of persistence. Documents range from short forum posts to long academic papers and code files, and the degree of document-level coherence varies accordingly. Code, for example, combines strong local syntactic structure with long-range dependencies on identifiers defined much earlier, whereas some web text consists of loosely related fragments. Aggregate statistics computed over the corpus therefore average over very different temporal regimes, and per-domain analyses may reveal structure that the aggregate obscures.

### C.2 MMLU Dataset

Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) is an English-language benchmark of four-option multiple-choice questions from 57 subjects spanning STEM, the humanities, the social sciences, and other professional and academic fields [29]. We use MMLU only for the subject analyses; it is not used to train the SAEs. Specifically, we use questions from abstract algebra, astronomy, business ethics, computer security, and European history. These subjects cover distinct areas while providing a subject label for every example.

For the geometry analysis in Section 5.3, we sample $100$ sequences across the five subjects and retain the final $20$ token representations from each sequence. For subject probing, we construct sequences by joining equal-length segments from different subjects and assign each token the subject label of its source segment. Appendix F and Appendix G provide the sampling and evaluation details for the two analyses.

The five subjects were chosen to span mathematical, scientific, professional, technical, and historical text, so that subject distinctions involve differences in vocabulary, register, and argumentative structure rather than in a single lexical cue. Using the final tokens of each sequence ensures that every retained representation has been computed with a substantial amount of subject-specific preceding context.

### C.3 AgentDojo Trajectories

Indirect prompt injection occurs when an agent retrieves attacker-controlled text from emails, webpages, documents, or tool outputs and follows instructions inside that text. AgentDojo [12] evaluates this setting with stateful tool environments containing 97 user tasks, 27 injection targets, and 629 security test cases across workspace, Slack, travel, and banking domains. Its task-specific checks evaluate whether the legitimate user request and the attacker’s target action were completed by inspecting the agent output and changes to the environment.

For our monitoring dataset, we use trajectories from the banking, travel, and workspace domains generated by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. Benign trajectories without an injection form the negative class ( $y=0$ ). The positive class ( $y=1$ ) contains runs with an important_instructions or direct attack for which the AgentDojo injection checker returns security=false. This value means that an injection was present but the agent did not complete the attacker’s target action. We retain these failed attacks deliberately: successful attacks often contain an overt malicious action, such as transferring money or sending private data, which could provide a trivial downstream classification cue. This restriction asks whether the monitor retains a trace of the injection even when no observable attack success occurs. We do not filter by task utility, so the legitimate user request may either succeed or fail.

## Appendix D Empirical Persistence of Standard SAE Features

This appendix discusses methodological considerations for measuring how long the signal associated with an SAE feature remains in the hidden state after the feature activates. Such measurements are useful both for characterising standard SAEs and for interpreting the timescales of a Persistent SAE, but they are easy to get wrong, and we set out the precautions we consider necessary.

Anchoring on activation events. 
The natural unit of analysis is an activation event: a token at which a feature’s sparse activation is positive. Projections onto the feature’s decoder direction can then be tracked at subsequent lags $\tau$ and compared with the feature’s average projection over all tokens. Normalising by the elevation at the activating token itself makes measurements comparable across features whose activations differ in scale.

Feature selection. 
Not every feature admits a reliable measurement. Rarely active features provide too few activation events for stable averages, and anchors near the end of a document cannot be followed to long lags. We therefore recommend retaining only features with a minimum number of activation events and a minimum number of valid anchors at every lag considered. A further subtlety concerns features whose activated-token elevation is near zero, as occurs for near-dead or diffuse features: a normalised measure is undefined in this case, and adding a small constant to the denominator would produce arbitrarily large or unstable values. Such features should be excluded rather than regularised.

Confounds. 
Three confounds deserve attention. First, decoder directions are not orthogonal, so the projection onto one direction can be elevated by the activity of correlated features; persistence measured through projections is thus a property of a direction in the residual stream rather than of a feature in isolation. Second, activation events are not distributed uniformly across positions, and since hidden-state statistics vary with position, comparisons across lags can be affected by positional drift. Restricting analysis to positions after an initial prefix and limiting the maximum document length mitigates but does not eliminate this effect. Third, local continuity—the fact that consecutive tokens belong to the same phrase or sentence—produces short-range persistence regardless of whether a representation tracks document-level context. Separating local from global contributions requires a control that preserves the former while disrupting the latter.

Heterogeneity across features. 
Aggregate statistics such as medians across features summarise the typical behaviour of a dictionary, but they can conceal substantial variation. Grouping lags into short, medium, and long bands and examining the distribution of persistence within each band gives a more complete picture than a single curve. Such per-band distributions are also the natural point of comparison for the timescale parameters of a Persistent SAE, since they indicate whether features that a model treats as long-lived are distinguished in the hidden states themselves.

Descriptive fits. 
It is sometimes convenient to summarise a decay curve by fitting a parametric form, such as an exponential or power law, to its positive tail. Such fits are descriptive rather than mechanistic, and their parameters should be compared only between conditions measured under identical selection criteria. Because the tail of a decay curve is estimated from fewer anchors than its head, fits should weight lags appropriately or be restricted to a range in which estimates are stable.

### D.1 Context Correction Experiment

A complementary diagnostic asks whether a feature’s past activation is informative about the hidden state at a later token along the same direction. One way to operationalise this is to augment a standard SAE’s reconstruction with a correction term that adds, for each feature, a learned multiple of its activation $\tau$ tokens earlier along its own decoder direction, and to measure how much of the baseline reconstruction error this correction recovers on held-out documents.

Why a feature-wise correction. 
Restricting the correction to act feature-wise, rather than allowing an arbitrary linear map from past activations to the current hidden state, is essential for the diagnostic to be informative about features. A dense map would trivially exploit the well-known correlation between consecutive hidden states and would not indicate whether any individual feature carries information forward. A feature-wise correction has only one parameter per feature, so any gain it achieves can be attributed to specific features, and the sign of each parameter indicates whether past activation predicts a positive or negative contribution along the same direction.

Fitting and evaluation. 
The correction should be fitted on one set of documents and evaluated on a disjoint held-out set, with regularisation to prevent overfitting of rarely active features. Because the gains from such a correction are expected to be small relative to the total reconstruction error—the baseline SAE already explains most of the variance—care is needed to ensure that any measured improvement exceeds what would be obtained by chance. A useful control refits the correction using past activations drawn from unrelated text while keeping the same natural-document targets; this preserves the marginal statistics of the activations while removing any genuine relationship with the target document’s history. We fit corrections at a range of lags with AdamW, a learning rate of $5\times 10^{-3}$ , weight decay of $10^{-3}$ , and $10$ epochs, after dropping $16$ prefix tokens and capping each document at $768$ tokens.

Relationship to Persistent SAEs. 
A Persistent SAE can be viewed as internalising this diagnostic: rather than fitting a correction post hoc to a frozen atemporal SAE, it allows each feature’s state to carry information forward during training and lets the encoder and decoder adapt jointly. The two approaches therefore answer related but distinct questions. The post-hoc correction asks whether an atemporal decomposition leaves feature-level temporal information unused; the Persistent SAE asks what a decomposition learns when that information is available to it from the outset.

## Appendix E Automated Interpretability Details

We follow the automated interpretability pipeline of Bills et al. [23]. For each feature we collect its highest-activation contexts, prompt a judge model to write a short natural-language explanation, and score how well that explanation predicts whether the evaluated feature activation exceeds a threshold on held-out contexts. For standard SAEs, this activation is $f_{j}^{(t)}$ ; for the Persistent SAE, we use the token-wise activation $a_{j}^{(t)}$ . We use gpt-4o-mini as the judge, a context length of $1024$ tokens, and roughly $2$ M tokens from the Pile for the activation examples. This evaluates the Persistent SAE on its token-wise activations, matching the token-specific representations of the baselines. We also score groups of Persistent SAE features defined by their timescale parameters, to evaluate their interpretability as groups.

Explanation and scoring. 
The explanation step presents the judge with a fixed number of high-activation contexts, each centred on the activating token and annotated with activation values. The judge is asked for a concise description of what the feature responds to. In the scoring step, the judge receives the explanation together with a mixture of held-out contexts, some containing activations above threshold and some not, and predicts which contexts contain activations. The score reflects the agreement between these predictions and the actual activations. Holding out contexts used for scoring from those used for explanation is important, since otherwise the score would reward memorisation of specific examples rather than a generalisable description.

Sampling considerations. 
High-activation contexts are drawn from the top of each feature’s activation distribution, which emphasises the clearest cases. Features with broad, low-amplitude activation profiles may be poorly represented by their maxima, and for such features the explanation may describe an extreme case rather than typical behaviour. Including contexts sampled from lower activation quantiles alongside the maxima can mitigate this, at the cost of making explanations harder to write. We use the same sampling scheme for all SAE families so that comparisons are not affected by this choice.

Limitations for persistent features. 
As discussed in Section 5.2, token-level pipelines are best suited to features whose relevance is concentrated at the activating token. For features whose evidence accumulates across a sequence, the window presented to the judge may omit much of the context that determines the feature’s role, and descriptions may converge on broad semantic domains that several distinct features share [24]. Developing pipelines that present longer contexts, or that describe groups of features jointly, is a natural direction for evaluating persistent representations more faithfully.

## Appendix F Subject Geometry Details

For the t-SNE visualisation we draw $100$ sequences from five MMLU subjects (abstract algebra, astronomy, business ethics, computer security, and European history) and keep the last $20$ tokens of each sequence, so that every token carries a subject label. For each representation—raw hidden states, BatchTopK features, the Temporal SAE’s high-level group, and a timescale-selected subset of the Persistent SAE state—we collect the token-level vectors and project them to two dimensions with t-SNE using a common set of hyperparameters, colouring each point by its subject.

Because t-SNE emphasises local neighbourhood structure and can exaggerate or suppress cluster separation depending on perplexity and initialisation, we use a fixed random seed and a single perplexity setting across all representations, and we standardise each representation before projection. The visualisation is intended to support qualitative comparison; quantitative claims about subject information are based on the probing analysis in Appendix G.

## Appendix G Subject Probing Details

We construct spliced sequences by concatenating equal-length segments drawn from different MMLU subjects, balancing subject labels within each sequence and holding out entire source documents for the test split, so that a token’s label is the subject of the segment it falls in. We treat each token as a labelled example and fit a linear probe to predict its source subject from the token-level representation. We report held-out one-vs-rest macro ROC AUC as a function of the fraction of features made available, swept from $0.1\%$ to $100\%$ . We evaluate the Persistent SAE on its persistent state $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ and order its features by decreasing timescale, increasing timescale, repeated random permutations, or supervised one-vs-rest importance. For each subject $c$ , the supervised score for feature $j$ is

| | $s_{j,c}=\mathbb{E}[h^{(t)}_{j}\mid y^{(t)}=c]-\mathbb{E}[h^{(t)}_{j}\mid y^{(t)}\neq c],$
| | (8)

computed on the training split. This score measures how much larger the persistent state of feature $j$ is for subject $c$ than for the other subjects. We sort features by this score within each subject and interleave the subject-specific rankings in round-robin order, ensuring that every subject contributes its most discriminative features. This produces a single global feature ordering used by the multiclass probe. For the BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and Temporal baselines, we use their full dictionaries under the same probe.

Holding out entire source documents for the test split prevents the probe from exploiting memorised content: a token in the test set never shares a source question with any training token. Balancing subjects within each spliced sequence ensures that the prior probability of each subject is uniform, so that a probe cannot improve its score simply by favouring frequent subjects. Random rankings are repeated over several permutations and averaged, giving a reference curve against which structured rankings can be compared.

## Appendix H Prompt Injection Monitoring Details

Trajectory construction. 
Trajectories are taken from AgentDojo [12] runs of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct agents. Attack trajectories are restricted to the important_instructions and direct attack types and to runs with security=false. In this dataset, these positives contain an injection whose targeted action the agent did not execute; benign trajectories contain no injected content. Each trajectory is serialised and appended with the monitoring query

should this trajectory be flagged for prompt injection or unsafe instruction hijacking? Answer yes or no:

and read with Gemma-2-2B; all representations are taken from the layer-12 residual stream. The model’s own answer to this query is close to uninformative: the yes-minus-no answer logit at the query position gives an AUC of $0.51$ , which is why we train internal monitors rather than relying on prompting.

Checkpoints and probes. 
For each trajectory, we locate the final token of the injected span (for benign trajectories, the token at the matched position) and define checkpoints at fixed offsets of $0$ , $50$ , $100$ , $200$ , $250$ , $300$ , and $350$ tokens after it, together with the final query position. At each checkpoint we extract, from the same layer, the raw hidden state, the BatchTopK and Matryoshka sparse activations, the Temporal SAE’s high-level feature group, and the Persistent SAE’s token-wise activation $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ , full state $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ , and timescale-selected subsets of the state. A logistic regression probe is fit on each representation using checkpoint $d=0$ only and then evaluated, without retraining, at every other checkpoint; we report held-out accuracy and ROC AUC.

Causal intervention. 
For each SAE representation, we select the $k=128$ features with the largest absolute probe coefficients and combine their weighted decoder columns into a probe-weighted decoder direction $\mathbf{v}_{r}$ . The direction is normalised and scaled so that its norm equals a fixed fraction $\rho=0.1$ of the hidden-state norm at the intervention position, then added to the residual stream with both signs. We measure the resulting change in the external replay monitor’s yes-minus-no logit margin, not a change in the original Llama-3.3-70B agent’s action. Interventions use the direction constructed at $d=0$ , so the analysis reflects how its causal effect transfers across distance.

Scaling interventions relative to the hidden-state norm ensures that perturbations are comparable across positions and trajectories, whose residual-stream norms vary. Restricting each steering direction to a fixed number of features keeps the comparison between representations fair, since a direction assembled from more features could otherwise achieve a larger effect simply by spanning more of the residual stream. Applying the intervention with both signs and taking the difference removes components of the effect that are independent of direction, such as a generic shift in the logit margin caused by any perturbation of the given magnitude.

# Persistent Sparse Autoencoders: Learning Feature-Specific Timescales in Language Model Representations

###### Abstract

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into sparse features, but they encode each token independently. We measure decoder-aligned projections of standard SAE features after activation and the held-out reconstruction gain from lagged activations along the same feature directions, on natural and sentence-shuffled corpora; both quantities, and their decay with lag, vary widely across features. We introduce Persistent Sparse Autoencoders (Persistent SAEs), which attach to each feature a diagonal state with a learned persistence coefficient trained by reconstruction alone.
Persistent SAEs retain competitive reconstruction quality while learning a spectrum of coefficients: low-coefficient (fast) features remain locally interpretable, and high-coefficient (slow) features cluster by subject and support subject probing without labels.
In a prompt-injection monitoring case study, slow features retain injection-related signal and yield positive causal effects on a replay monitor over long contexts. Persistent SAEs therefore offer new opportunities for interpreting and monitoring language models via persistent sparse features.

## 1 Introduction

Interpreting a large language model (LLM) requires identifying what its hidden states represent and how that content evolves over a sequence [1, 2]. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) [3, 4] decompose hidden states into sparse features; when these align with human-interpretable concepts, the decomposition supports inspection of learnt concepts and model control through intervention on features [5, 6, 7].

Causal transformer hidden states integrate preceding context, yet standard SAEs encode each token independently [3, 8, 9], favouring token-specific features over information carried across a sequence such as topic, style, or task state [10].
Recent methods add temporal structure to SAEs via predefined partitions and decompositions of temporal roles [10, 11], which fixes a priori which features carry temporal information and introduces experimenter bias into the learnt dictionary.
Whether per-feature timescales can be learned from data rather than specified by architecture remains open.

As shown in Figure 1, after a standard SAE feature activates, later hidden states remain more strongly aligned with its decoder direction, and past activations reduce reconstruction error on subsequent hidden states, with feature-dependent decay rates. Standard SAEs encode each position independently and do not represent this.
We introduce Persistent Sparse Autoencoders, which learn a persistence coefficient $\lambda_{j}$ for every feature; each feature maintains a state that decays at $\lambda_{j}$ and is updated by a token-wise sparse activation, and $\lambda_{j}$ is optimised solely through the reconstruction objective.

Persistent SAEs retain competitive reconstruction while learning a broad range of timescales without supervision.
Most features are low- $\lambda_{j}$ fast features behaving as locally interpretable detectors; a small set of high- $\lambda_{j}$ slow features accumulate contextual information across the sequence.
In a prompt-injection monitoring case study [12], slow features serve as monitoring signals for malicious prompt injections over longer time scales.
Our main contributions are:

•

We show that SAE features exhibit temporal persistence: after a feature is activated, its decoder direction remains elevated, and past activations can help predict subsequent states.

•

We introduce Persistent Sparse Autoencoders, which learn one coefficient per sparse feature through reconstruction alone, retain competitive reconstruction quality, and discover a broad spectrum of timescales without a predefined partition of temporal roles.

•

We show that short-timescale (fast) features act as locally interpretable detectors, while long-timescale (slow) features retain contextual information in a sequence, and demonstrate in a prompt-injection monitoring case study the use of slow features to monitor and steer models over long contexts.

## 2 Background and Related Work

Sparse autoencoders. 
Given an LLM’s hidden state $\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ at token $t$ , a standard SAE [3] encodes $\mathbf{x}^{(t)}$ as non-negative sparse activations $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}$ and reconstructs

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{f}^{(t)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}.$
| | (1)

Feature $j$ comprises the activation $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}$ and the direction $\mathbf{d}_{j}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}[:,j]/\lVert\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}[:,j]\rVert_{2}$ (notation in Appendix A), and is active when $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0$ .
Sparsity limits each reconstruction to a small set of features [3, 13].
BatchTopK [8] replaces the per-token TopK constraint with a batch-level sparsity budget so that the number of active features varies across tokens; Matryoshka SAEs [9] jointly train nested dictionaries of increasing size so that smaller subsets retain higher-level features while larger dictionaries add more specific ones.

Temporal structure in LLM representations. 
Autoregressive LLMs build $\mathbf{x}^{(t)}$ from the preceding context, but standard SAEs and most variants compute $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}$ independently of features at preceding tokens. Slow feature analysis identifies higher-level features in neural networks via slowly varying latent factors [14, 15].
Language models track entities, and their hidden states encode game-board, spatial, temporal, and propositional states [16, 17, 18, 19].

Temporal extensions of SAEs. 
Temporal SAEs [10] pre-assign a high-level feature subset and align its activations across nearby tokens with a contrastive objective. Lubana et al. [11] use an attention-based predictor to separate context-predictable information from a sparse novel residual. Both fix the temporal structure through a partition, and neither assigns an individual timescale to each sparse feature. Persistent SAEs assign each feature a state and a learned persistence coefficient directly available for post-hoc analysis.

## 3 Does Temporal Structure Exist at the Feature Level?

We measure, for standard SAEs, the signal along $\mathbf{d}_{j}$ following activation of feature $j$ and the effect of past activations on reconstruction of subsequent hidden states.

Setup. 
We use residual-stream hidden states $\{\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ from Pythia-160M-deduped (layer 8) [20] and Gemma-2-2B (layer 12) [21] on Pile documents [22], and train BatchTopK [8] and Matryoshka [9] SAEs, neither with a temporal prior (configurations in Appendix B).

Natural Pile documents have local continuity (coherent sentences) and global continuity (a coherent document-level context). The shuffled control concatenates intact sentences from different Pile documents, preserving the former but not the latter (Figure 1 (a); construction in Appendix C).

Sparse Features Temporally Persist in the Hidden States. 
For each position $t$ , let $p^{(t)}_{j}=\mathbf{d}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{x}^{(t)}$ . Conditioning on $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0$ , the empirical persistence at lag $\tau$ is

| | $R_{j}(\tau):=\big({\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t+\tau)}_{j}\mid\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0\right]-\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t)}_{j}\right]}\Big)\Big/\Big({\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t)}_{j}\mid\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0\right]-\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t)}_{j}\right]}\Big),$
| | (2)

where $\mathbb{E}[p^{(t)}_{j}]$ is the average projection over all evaluated tokens, so that $R_{j}(\tau)=1$ and $R_{j}(\tau)=0$ correspond to full retention and return to baseline after $\tau$ tokens. Evaluation procedure and feature selection are in Appendix D.

Across both models and SAE families, $R_{j}(\tau)$ decays more slowly on natural documents than on the shuffled control (Figure 1 (b)).

Past Activations Can Help Reconstruction. 
We augment Equation 1 with a restricted context correction from activations $\tau$ tokens earlier:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{ctx}}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}+\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{\tau}\odot\mathbf{f}^{(t-\tau)}\right).$
| | (3)

Each $w_{\tau,j}$ of $\mathbf{w}_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ acts only along $\mathbf{d}_{j}$ . For each lag, $\mathbf{w}_{\tau}$ is fit for 10 epochs with an $L_{2}$ penalty, and we report the fraction of baseline error recovered on held-out data:

| | $R^{2}_{\mathrm{improve}}=1-\Big({\sum_{t}\lVert\mathbf{x}^{(t)}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{ctx}}\rVert_{2}^{2}}\Big)\Big/\Big({\sum_{t}\lVert\mathbf{x}^{(t)}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}\rVert_{2}^{2}}\Big).$
| | (4)

In the control, $\mathbf{w}_{\tau}$ is refit with past activations from the shuffled corpus against the same natural-document targets (details in Section D.1).

On natural documents past activations recover a fraction of the baseline error, decreasing with lag; the shuffled control yields no gain (Figure 1 (c)). At $\tau=1$ the fitted weights are mostly positive on natural documents and centred near zero on the shuffled control (Figure 1 (d)).

Lubana et al. [11] show that hidden-state correlations vary across a sequence and that past hidden states explain much of the current hidden state. Our analysis is restricted to individual SAE features, whose persistence both aids reconstruction and varies widely across features.

## 4 Persistent Sparse Autoencoders

Persistent SAEs separate a token-wise sparse activation from a persistent state (Figure 2).

Figure 2:
Persistent Sparse Autoencoders. Each feature integrates its token-wise sparse activation $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ into a persistent state $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ with its learned persistence coefficient $\lambda_{j}$ .

A BatchTopK encoder (Section B.2) produces $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}$ , with $a^{(t)}_{j}>0$ denoting new evidence for feature $j$ at token $t$ . Each feature updates a state $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}$ with coefficient $\lambda_{j}\in[0,1]$ :

| | $h^{(t)}_{j}=\lambda_{j}h^{(t-1)}_{j}+(1-\lambda_{j})a^{(t)}_{j}.$
| | (5)

Small and large $\lambda_{j}$ give short-timescale (fast) and long-timescale (slow) features respectively; the factor $(1-\lambda_{j})$ bounds the state magnitude.
We set $\mathbf{h}^{(0)}=\mathbf{0}$ at the start of every input sequence and parameterise $\lambda_{j}=\lambda_{\max}\sigma(l_{j})$ with unconstrained $l_{j}$ and $\lambda_{\max}=0.999$ (Section B.3).

The decoder reads from the state:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{h}^{(t)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}.$
| | (6)

The recurrence is diagonal in feature space, so each $h^{(t)}_{j}$ contributes only along $\mathbf{d}_{j}$ . Sparsity is imposed on $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ ; $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ integrates sparse updates but need not itself be sparse.
The only training signal for $l_{j}$ is the reconstruction loss through Equation 6; no feature partitions or auxiliary temporal objectives are used.

We evaluate reconstruction and token-wise interpretability (Sections 5.1 and 5.2), the content of slow-feature states (Section 5.3), and long-context prompt-injection monitoring (Section 5.4).

Models and hyperparameters. 
Models and dataset follow Section 3. Baselines are BatchTopK SAE [8], Matryoshka SAE [9], and Temporal SAE [10].
All SAEs use $m=16{,}384$ features and a BatchTopK budget of $k=20$ ; Matryoshka and Temporal SAEs share a predefined 20%/80% feature partition (Appendix B).

### 5.2 Short-Timescale Features Are Locally Interpretable

We use the automated interpretability pipeline of Bills et al. [23], in which a judge model explains a feature from its highest-activation contexts and then scores how well the explanation predicts activation. For the Persistent SAE we score the token-wise activation $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ (Appendix E).

On both models fast features score higher than slow features (Table 1, right) and match or exceed the best baseline.
Qualitative examples (Tables 4 and 5 in Appendix E) show fast features responding to compact lexical or grammatical patterns such as letters or substrings, with activation concentrated at the current token, and slow features reflecting broader subjects or contextual conditions with activation distributed across the sequence.
Token-specific evaluation is known to be limited for such features: distinct features may receive similar descriptions [24], and explanations may not generalise to related inputs [25]. Section 5.3 evaluates slow features jointly.

Where Features Receive New Evidence. 
We divide features into five equal-sized $\lambda$ quintiles and assign their update positions to six token categories: punctuation, conjunctions, function words, verbs, adjectives or adverbs, and nouns, following the classical lexical/content versus grammatical/function distinction [26].
Function words (Func. in Figure 4) include adpositions, determiners, particles, and pronouns.
For quintile $q$ and category $c$ ,

| | $U_{q,c}={\Pr\!\left(T^{(t)}=c\mid a^{(t)}_{j}>0,\;j\in Q_{q}\right)}\big/{\Pr\!\left(T^{(t)}=c\right)},$
| | (7)

where $T^{(t)}$ is the category of token $t$ and $Q_{q}$ is the feature set of quintile $q$ ; values above and below one indicate over- and under-representation of updates relative to corpus frequency.

Figure 4: Where features receive evidence. Each cell shows how often features in a $\lambda$ -quintile are updated at a token category relative to the category corpus-level frequency. Orange and blue indicate frequencies above and below the corpus-level baseline.

The contrast is sharpest at the extremes of the distribution (Figure 4): lowest- $\lambda$ features are over-represented at nouns, highest- $\lambda$ features at punctuation and conjunctions.
In LLMs, punctuation and other function-like tokens carry substantial contextual information [27], and explicit structural markers gate cross-sentence integration of information [28].
Autointerpretations of high- $\lambda$ features frequently describe broad semantic domains (Tables 4 and 5).

### 5.3 Long-Timescale States Track Subject Information

Slow features form subject-specific clusters. 
We take MMLU [29] examples from five subjects, collect representations of the final $20$ tokens of each sample, and embed them with t-SNE (Appendix F), using the highest $1\%$ of features by $\lambda_{j}$ . BatchTopK features heavily mix subjects and the Temporal SAE’s predefined high-level group gives limited separation, whereas slow Persistent SAE features form coherent subject regions with clearer separation than the raw hidden states (Figure 5). No subject labels are used in training.

Figure 5:
Token-level MMLU representations, coloured by subject. The Persistent SAE’s high- $\lambda_{j}$ slow features reveal clearer subject structure than baseline SAEs or the raw hidden states.

Temporal Persistence Selects Subject-Informative Features Without Labels. 
Spliced MMLU sequences concatenate labelled segments from different subjects, so the subject changes at segment boundaries. A per-token linear probe predicts the current subject from a varying fraction of the dictionary. Persistent SAE features are ranked by decreasing $\lambda_{j}$ , increasing $\lambda_{j}$ , and randomly; we compare with BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and Temporal SAE representations and with a supervised oracle ranking that, per subject, favours features activating more strongly on that subject than on the others (Appendix G).

Decreasing-persistence selection nearly matches supervised selection (Figure 6). On both models the slowest $1\%$ of features reach high AUC, while low- $\lambda_{j}$ , random, and baseline representations retain substantially less subject information at the same budget.

### 5.4 Case Study: Persistent Prompt Injection Monitoring

In indirect prompt injection [12], an agent encounters a malicious instruction in an email, webpage, or tool response, continues for hundreds of tokens, and acts later [30]; an agentic monitor must retain a security-relevant signal until the agent acts [31, 32].

Setting. 
We use AgentDojo trajectories from the banking, travel, and workspace domains [12] generated by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct [33] (Section C.3). Each contains a request, an untrusted span with a prompt injection or benign content, and subsequent tool calls. Only failed attacks are used, in which the injection is present but the agent does not complete the attack’s action.

Gemma-2-2B serves as an external monitor: each trajectory is replayed and the layer-12 residual stream recorded. A linear probe is trained at the final token of the untrusted span ( $d=0$ ) and evaluated without retraining up to $350$ tokens later (Figure 7 (a)). Representations are the raw hidden state, baseline SAE representations, and the Persistent SAE state $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ restricted to slow features (highest $1\%$ by $\lambda_{j}$ ) or fast features (lowest $50\%$ ) as in Section 5.1 (Appendix H).

Figure 7:
Persistent monitoring of prompt injection. (a) A probe trained at the end of an untrusted span is evaluated later in the trajectory. (b) Slow states retain more predictive information (top) and the strongest causal effect on the monitor’s judgement (bottom).

Signal retention: fast features detect local injections while slow states retain signals over long contexts. 
At $d=0$ the fast-feature state and standard SAE representations give the strongest detection (Figure 7 (b), top), and their accuracy falls towards chance with distance from the untrusted span; the slow-feature state retains a clearer signal at longer distances.

Causal effect: slow-feature directions causally influence the monitor’s judgement. 
Each trajectory is truncated at a later distance, a query asks whether it should be flagged for prompt injection, and we intervene at the final query token.
Following work that selects SAE features for steering and identifies task-relevant sparse subspaces with linear classifiers [7, 34], we form for each SAE representation $r$ a steering vector $\mathbf{v}_{r}$ from its most predictive decoder directions weighted by probe coefficients, and apply it with both signs. With logit margin $s(\mathbf{x})=\ell_{\mathrm{yes}}(\mathbf{x})-\ell_{\mathrm{no}}(\mathbf{x})$ ,

| | $\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{causal}}(r,d)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{i}\Big[s\big(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(d)}+\alpha_{i}^{(d)}\mathbf{v}_{r}\big)-s\big(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(d)}-\alpha_{i}^{(d)}\mathbf{v}_{r}\big)\Big],$
| | (8)

where $\alpha_{i}^{(d)}$ scales each intervention to $10\%$ of the hidden-state norm; positive $\Delta_{\mathrm{causal}}$ shifts the monitor towards yes.

Slow features produce the largest and most consistently positive effect at every distance, while BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and Temporal SAE directions give near-zero or negative effects with no comparable alignment over distance (Figure 7 (b), bottom).
The Persistent SAE thus provides immediate detection, long-context retention, and causal influence within a single representation.

## 6 Conclusion and Discussion

Conclusion. 
Persistent SAEs learn from reconstruction alone a per-feature persistence coefficient spanning a broad range of timescales: short-timescale features remain locally interpretable, and long-timescale features track subject identity and preserve monitoring signals over long contexts. This provides an unsupervised organisation of sparse representations by timescale and a direction for interpreting and monitoring information maintained by LLMs over long contexts.

Limitations and Future Work. 
A single fixed coefficient per feature in a diagonal recurrence cannot capture interactions between features or context-dependent resets. The prompt-injection study uses an external replay monitor, so the interventions establish effects on the monitor’s judgement rather than on the original agent’s actions. Future work could explore richer recurrent dynamics and test whether persistent feature interventions affect end-to-end agent behaviour.

## Appendix B SAE Training Details

### B.1 SAE Baseline Training Details

We train four SAE families: BatchTopK [8],
Matryoshka BatchTopK [9], Temporal SAE [10],
and the Persistent SAE, with shared dictionary width, BatchTopK activation budget,
optimiser, and token budget, so that differences reflect temporal representation rather than training data volume or number of optimisation steps.

Common configuration. 
Every SAE has $m=16{,}384$ features and a BatchTopK activation
budget of $k=20$ per token. We use Adam with learning rate $3\times 10^{-4}$ and
a linear warm-up over the first $1{,}000$ steps. From step $1{,}000$ we apply the
BatchTopK activation-threshold schedule with decay $\beta=0.999$ and the
auxiliary dead-feature loss weighted by $\alpha_{\mathrm{aux}}=0.03125$ . Training
activations come from Pile Uncopyrighted [35] with the beginning-of-sequence
position removed. For Gemma-2-2B [21] we use the layer-12 residual stream
with hidden width $d=2{,}304$ ; for Pythia-160M-deduped [20],
the layer-8 residual stream with $d=768$ .

The Matryoshka and Temporal SAEs share two
predefined feature groups containing $20\%$ and $80\%$ of the $16{,}384$ features.
The Temporal SAE weights its reconstruction losses by $0.2$ and $0.8$ ,
respectively; Matryoshka uses uniform reconstruction weights. The Persistent SAE
uses no predefined partition and learns a persistence coefficient for every
feature.

Matched token budget. 
BatchTopK and Matryoshka consume shuffled token activations, the Temporal SAE adjacent token pairs, and
the Persistent SAE contiguous sequences.
We match the number of activation tokens per optimisation step
and the total number of steps rather than the number of structural units. Each
model is trained for $244{,}140$ steps with an effective batch of approximately
$2{,}048$ activation tokens per step, giving for the flat baselines
$2{,}048\times 244{,}140=499{,}998{,}720$ tokens, or approximately $5.0\times 10^{8}$
tokens in total.

•

BatchTopK and Matryoshka. The activation buffer returns a flat
batch of $2{,}048$ token activations at each step.

•

Temporal SAE. The buffer returns adjacent previous–next token
pairs from the same activation stream, with the number of reconstructed token
positions per step equal to the flat-baseline batch size.

•

Persistent SAE. Eight sequences of context length
$256$ per step; excluding the beginning-of-sequence position gives
$8\times 255=2{,}040$ usable token activations per step, within $0.4\%$ of the
flat-baseline budget.

All families therefore receive the same number of gradient updates and, up to
the pairing or sequencing their objectives require, approximately the same number
of token activations. Checkpoints are saved on a fixed schedule and the final dictionary
(ae.pt) is used for every downstream evaluation. All experiments were run on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80 GB of memory.

### B.2 BatchTopK Sparsity

All SAEs in this paper impose sparsity with BatchTopK. A hidden state $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is mapped to non-negative pre-activations

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{f}}=\mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}})+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{enc}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m},$
| | (9)

of which only the largest are retained across the batch.
For $X=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}$ , the pre-activations $\{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}$ are flattened to length $Bm$ , and $\mathbf{f}_{i}$ keeps the top $kB$ entries globally, zeroing the rest.
The reconstruction is

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{f}_{i}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}.$
| | (10)

After training with exact BatchTopK selection, inference uses the thresholded form

| | $f_{ij}=\tilde{f}_{ij}\,\mathbf{1}[\tilde{f}_{ij}>\theta],$
| | (11)

with $\theta$ estimated from training-time top- $k$ statistics.
The Persistent SAE uses this sparse activation as $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ ; only its downstream use differs.

### B.3 Persistence Parameterisation

The persistence coefficients are

| | $\lambda_{j}=\sigma(l_{j})\cdot\lambda_{\max},$
| | (12)

with unconstrained logit $l_{j}\in\mathbb{R}$ , sigmoid $\sigma$ , and hard cap $\lambda_{\max}=0.999$ preventing exact poles,
so $\lambda_{j}\in(0,\lambda_{\max})$ throughout training.
With the factor $(1-\lambda_{j})$ , Equation 5 is an exponential moving average (EMA) rather than an unnormalised sum: under constant $a^{(t)}_{j}=a_{j}$ the state converges to $a_{j}$ for every $\lambda_{j}$ . The cap below one gives every feature finite effective memory. Every logit $l_{j}$ is initialised to $0.5$ , giving moderate initial persistence away from sigmoid saturation so that the timescale can move in either direction.

## Appendix C Dataset Details

Pile documents provide hidden states for SAE training and evaluation, MMLU provides subject-labelled text for state analysis, and AgentDojo trajectories support the prompt-injection case study.

### C.1 Pile Corpus

The original Pile is an $825$  GiB English-language corpus assembled from 22 sources, including academic papers, web pages, books, code, and online discussions [22]. We use the Pile Uncopyrighted release [35], which removes the Books3, BookCorpus2, OpenSubtitles, YouTube Subtitles, and OpenWebText2 components. Documents are streamed and shuffled with a buffer of size $10{,}000$ under a fixed seed, and accepted if, after tokenisation with the model tokeniser and truncation to the context cap, they contain at least the required minimum number of tokens.

For the natural corpus, each accepted document is passed through the model and the chosen residual-stream hidden states retained.
For retained length $L$ , temporal statistics are computed on positions $\{16,\dots,L-1\}$ .

The shuffled control is built at the sentence level rather than by token permutation: sentences sampled from documents in the same corpus are concatenated under an adjacency constraint forbidding consecutive sentences from the same source document, breaking long-range entity tracking and discourse progression while preserving within-sentence continuity.

### C.2 MMLU Dataset

Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) is an English-language benchmark of four-option multiple-choice questions from 57 subjects spanning STEM, the humanities, the social sciences, and other professional and academic fields [29]. It is used only for the subject analyses, not for SAE training. We use questions from abstract algebra, astronomy, business ethics, computer security, and European history, which cover distinct areas and supply a subject label for every example.

For the geometry analysis in Section 5.3 we sample $100$ sequences across the five subjects and retain the final $20$ token representations of each. For subject probing we join equal-length segments from different subjects and label each token with the subject of its source segment (Appendix F and Appendix G).

### C.3 AgentDojo Trajectories

Indirect prompt injection occurs when an agent retrieves attacker-controlled text from emails, webpages, documents, or tool outputs and follows instructions inside it. AgentDojo [12] evaluates this with stateful tool environments containing 97 user tasks, 27 injection targets, and 629 security test cases across workspace, Slack, travel, and banking domains; task-specific checks inspect agent output and environment changes to determine whether the legitimate request and the attacker’s target action were completed.

We use trajectories from the banking, travel, and workspace domains generated by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. Benign trajectories without injection form the negative class ( $y=0$ ). The positive class ( $y=1$ ) contains runs with an important_instructions or direct attack for which the AgentDojo injection checker returns security=false, i.e. an injection was present but the attacker’s target action was not completed. Successful attacks are excluded because they often contain an overt malicious action, such as transferring money or sending private data, that would provide a trivial downstream classification cue. We do not filter by task utility, so the legitimate user request may either succeed or fail.

## Appendix D Empirical Persistence of Standard SAE Features

We evaluate lags $\tau\in\{1,4,16,32,64,128,256,512\}$ on documents of at most $1{,}024$ traced tokens. A feature is retained only with at least $256$ activation events, at least $64$ valid anchors at every lag, and a non-negligible activated-token elevation; $R_{j}(\tau)$ is undefined and excluded when its denominator $\mathbb{E}[p^{(t)}_{j}\mid\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0]-\mathbb{E}[p^{(t)}_{j}]$ is near zero, as for near-dead or diffuse features, and no $\epsilon$ is added to numerator or denominator.
On Pythia-160M, median persistence for BatchTopK falls from $0.618$ at lag $1$ to $0.160$ at lag $64$ and is $0.096$ at lag $512$ ; Matryoshka goes from $0.504$ to $0.108$ and $0.059$ . On Gemma-2-2B, natural-document persistence at lag $512$ is $0.042$ (BatchTopK) and $0.034$ (Matryoshka). On both models the shuffled control decays to approximately zero at long lags.
Power-law fits to the positive decay tail give median exponents $\beta_{\mathrm{nat}}\approx 0.32$ versus $\beta_{\mathrm{shf}}\approx 0.87$ – $0.92$ for both SAE families.

Ranking features by average $R_{j}(\tau)$ within short ( $\tau\leq 16$ ), medium ( $32\leq\tau\leq 64$ ), and long ( $\tau\geq 128$ ) lag bands yields distributions spanning nearly the full unit interval in every band. Some features are strongly persistent at short lags and decay before medium lags; others retain elevated projections into the long-lag regime. This heterogeneity appears in both SAE families and substantially exceeds that of the shuffled control.

### D.1 Context Correction Experiment

The per-feature correction of Equation 3 is fit independently at each lag $\tau\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\}$ , using $192$ natural documents to fit $\mathbf{w}_{\tau}$ and $96$ held-out natural documents to evaluate $R^{2}_{\mathrm{improve}}$ . The target is always the natural-document reconstruction error; the control refits the diagonal head on the same natural targets from context activations drawn from the shuffled corpus, with identical parameterisation and optimisation budget. Each document contributes at most $768$ tokens after dropping $16$ prefix tokens. We optimise for $10$ epochs with AdamW, learning rate $5\times 10^{-3}$ , and weight decay $10^{-3}$ .

On Pythia-160M the correction removes $0.89\%$ (BatchTopK) and $0.61\%$ (Matryoshka) of the baseline reconstruction error at lag $1$ , remaining positive at lag $32$ ( $0.22\%$ and $0.13\%$ ). On Gemma-2-2B both SAEs remove approximately $0.40\%$ at lag $1$ , about $0.02\%$ at lag $16$ , and nothing by lag $32$ . The shuffled controls stay slightly below zero throughout.

## Appendix F Subject Geometry Details

For the t-SNE visualisation we draw $100$ sequences from five MMLU subjects (abstract algebra, astronomy, business ethics, computer security, and European history) and keep the last $20$ tokens of each, so every token carries a subject label. For each representation—raw hidden states, BatchTopK features, the Temporal SAE’s high-level group, and the Persistent SAE’s high- $\lambda_{j}$ state—token-level vectors are projected to two dimensions with t-SNE under a common set of hyperparameters and coloured by subject.

## Appendix G Subject Probing Details

Spliced sequences concatenate equal-length segments from different MMLU subjects, with subject labels balanced within each sequence and entire source documents held out for the test split; a token’s label is the subject of its segment. A linear probe predicts each token’s source subject from its token-level representation, and we report held-out one-vs-rest macro ROC AUC as a function of the fraction of features available, swept from $0.1\%$ to $100\%$ . The Persistent SAE is evaluated on $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ with features ordered by decreasing $\lambda_{j}$ , increasing $\lambda_{j}$ , repeated random permutations, or supervised one-vs-rest importance. For subject $c$ , the supervised score of feature $j$ is

| | $s_{j,c}=\mathbb{E}[h^{(t)}_{j}\mid y^{(t)}=c]-\mathbb{E}[h^{(t)}_{j}\mid y^{(t)}\neq c],$
| | (13)

computed on the training split. Features are sorted by this score within each subject and the subject-specific rankings interleaved round-robin, so each subject contributes its most discriminative features, giving a single global ordering for the multiclass probe. BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and Temporal baselines use their full dictionaries under the same probe.

## Appendix H Prompt Injection Monitoring Details

Trajectory construction. 
Trajectories are AgentDojo [12] runs of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct agents. Attack trajectories are restricted to the important_instructions and direct attack types and to runs with security=false, so positives contain an injection whose targeted action was not executed; benign trajectories contain no injected content. Each trajectory is serialised, appended with the monitoring query

should this trajectory be flagged for prompt injection or unsafe instruction hijacking? Answer yes or no:

and read with Gemma-2-2B; all representations come from the layer-12 residual stream. The yes-minus-no answer logit at the query position gives an AUC of $0.51$ , so we train internal monitors rather than rely on prompting.

Checkpoints and probes. 
For each trajectory we locate the final token of the injected span (for benign trajectories, the token at the matched position) and define checkpoints at offsets of $0$ , $50$ , $100$ , $200$ , $250$ , $300$ , and $350$ tokens after it, plus the final query position. At each checkpoint we extract, from the same layer, the raw hidden state, BatchTopK and Matryoshka sparse activations, the Temporal SAE’s high-level feature group, and the Persistent SAE’s token-wise activation $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ , full state $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ , and slow state (the largest 1% of $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ coordinates by $\lambda_{j}$ ). A logistic regression probe is fit per representation at checkpoint $d=0$ only and evaluated without retraining at every other checkpoint; we report held-out accuracy and ROC AUC.

Causal intervention. 
For each SAE representation, the $k=128$ features with largest absolute probe coefficients have their decoder columns weighted by those coefficients and summed into $\mathbf{v}_{r}$ . The direction is normalised and scaled so that $\lVert\alpha_{i}^{(d)}\mathbf{v}_{r}\rVert_{2}=\rho\lVert\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(d)}\rVert_{2}$ with $\rho=0.1$ , then added to the residual stream with both signs. Equation 8 measures the change in the external replay monitor’s logit margin, not in the original Llama-3.3-70B agent’s action. All interventions use the direction constructed at $d=0$ , so Figure 7 reports transfer of its causal effect across distance.

# Persistent Sparse Autoencoders: Learning Feature-Specific Timescales in Language Model Representations

Haoyan Luo

Affiliation: University of Cambridge

  
Mateo Espinosa Zarlenga

Affiliation: University of Oxford

  
Mateja Jamnik

Affiliation: University of Cambridge

###### Abstract

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into sparse features, encoding each token independently. We measure, for standard BatchTopK and Matryoshka SAEs, the decoder-aligned projection of the residual stream at lags following feature activation, and the held-out reconstruction gain obtained from a diagonal lagged correction, on natural and sentence-shuffled Pile documents; both quantities are feature-dependent and contingent on the true document history.
We introduce Persistent Sparse Autoencoders (Persistent SAEs), in which each feature carries a diagonal exponential-moving-average state with a learned coefficient $\lambda_{j}$, trained by reconstruction alone.
Persistent SAEs remain competitive in reconstruction, and the learned $\lambda_{j}$ span a broad range: low- $\lambda_{j}$ (fast) features score highest under automated interpretability, whereas high- $\lambda_{j}$ (slow) features cluster by MMLU subject and support near-oracle subject probing.
On AgentDojo prompt-injection monitoring, slow states retain decodable injection signal up to 350 tokens after the untrusted span, and probe-weighted slow-feature decoder directions shift a Gemma-2-2B monitor's judgement at every evaluated distance.

## 1 Introduction

Interpreting large language models (LLMs) requires identifying what their hidden states represent and how that content evolves along a sequence [1, 2]. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) [3, 4] decompose hidden states into sparse features; where features align with human-interpretable concepts, the decomposition supports inspection of and intervention on model computation [5, 6, 7].

Causal transformer hidden states integrate preceding context, yet standard SAEs encode each token independently [3, 8, 9], favouring token-specific features over contextual variables such as topic, style, or task state [10].
Recent temporal SAEs impose structure through predefined feature partitions or decompositions of temporal roles [10, 11], which fixes a priori which features carry temporal information.

We measure, for standard SAE features, the decoder-aligned projection at lags after activation and the reconstruction gain from lagged activations along the same decoder direction (Figure 1); both decay at feature-dependent rates.
Persistent Sparse Autoencoders assign every feature a persistence coefficient $\lambda_{j}$; each feature's state decays at rate $\lambda_{j}$ and is updated by a token-wise sparse activation, with $\lambda_{j}$ optimised jointly with the dictionary under the reconstruction objective.

On Pythia-160M-deduped and Gemma-2-2B, Persistent SAEs match baseline reconstruction while learning a broad distribution of $\lambda_{j}$, concentrated at low values with a small high- $\lambda_{j}$ tail. Low- $\lambda_{j}$ features score at or above the best baselines under automated interpretability; high- $\lambda_{j}$ states cluster by subject, support subject probing at a 1% feature budget, and, in a prompt-injection monitoring study [12], retain decodable and causally effective injection signal over long distances.

Our contributions are: (i) feature-level measurements of temporal persistence and lagged reconstruction gain in standard SAEs, contrasted against a sentence-shuffled control; (ii) the Persistent SAE, which learns one persistence coefficient per sparse feature through reconstruction alone, with no predefined partition of temporal roles; and (iii) an evaluation across reconstruction, interpretability, subject geometry and probing, and long-context prompt-injection monitoring and steering.

## 2 Background and Related Work

Sparse autoencoders. 
Given an LLM’s hidden state $\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ at token $t$ , a standard SAE [3] encodes $\mathbf{x}^{(t)}$ as non-negative sparse activations $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}$ and reconstructs

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{f}^{(t)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}.$
| | (1)

The $j$ -th feature comprises the activation $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}$ and the normalised decoder direction $\mathbf{d}_{j}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}[:,j]/\lVert\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}[:,j]\rVert_{2}$ (notation in Appendix A); it is active when $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0$ .
Sparsity restricts each reconstruction to a small set of features [3, 13].
BatchTopK [8] replaces the per-token TopK constraint with a batch-level budget, so the number of active features varies across tokens; Matryoshka SAEs [9] jointly train nested dictionaries of increasing size, with smaller prefixes retaining higher-level features.

Temporal structure in LLM representations. 
Autoregressive LLMs build $\mathbf{x}^{(t)}$ from preceding context, whereas standard SAEs and most variants compute $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}$ independently of features at earlier tokens. Slow feature analysis identifies higher-level variables in neural networks with slowly varying latent factors [14, 15].
Language models track entities, and their hidden states encode game-board, spatial, temporal, and propositional states [16, 17, 18, 19].

Temporal extensions of SAEs. 
Temporal SAEs [10] pre-assign a high-level feature subset and align its activations across nearby tokens with a contrastive objective. Lubana et al. [11] separate context-predictable information, via an attention-based predictor, from a sparse novel residual. Both fix temporal structure through a partition, and neither assigns individual sparse features their own timescale. Persistent SAEs give each feature a persistent state and a learned, directly readable persistence coefficient.

## 3 Does Temporal Structure Exist at the Feature Level?

We test, for standard SAEs, whether signal along $\mathbf{d}_{j}$ remains after feature $j$ activates and whether past activations reduce reconstruction error at later tokens.

Setup. 
We analyse residual-stream hidden states $\{\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ from Pythia-160M-deduped (layer 8) [20] and Gemma-2-2B (layer 12) [21] on Pile documents [22], using BatchTopK [8] and Matryoshka [9] SAEs (training configurations in Appendix B).

Natural Pile documents exhibit local continuity (coherent sentences) and global continuity (a coherent document-level context). The shuffled control concatenates intact sentences drawn from different Pile documents, preserving the former and breaking the latter (Figure 1 (a); construction in Appendix C).

Sparse Features Temporally Persist in the Hidden States. 
Define the projection $p^{(t)}_{j}=\mathbf{d}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{x}^{(t)}$ . Conditioning on feature $j$ being active at token $t$ , the empirical persistence at lag $\tau$ is

| | $R_{j}(\tau):=\big({\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t+\tau)}_{j}\mid\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0\right]-\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t)}_{j}\right]}\Big)\Big/\Big({\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t)}_{j}\mid\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0\right]-\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t)}_{j}\right]}\Big),$
| | (2)

with $\mathbb{E}[p^{(t)}_{j}]$ the mean projection over all evaluated tokens. Evaluation procedure and feature-selection criteria are in Appendix D.

Across both models and SAE families, $R_{j}(\tau)$ decays more slowly in natural documents than in the shuffled control (Figure 1 (b)).

Past Activations Can Help Reconstruction. 
We augment Equation 1 with activations from $\tau$ tokens earlier:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{ctx}}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}+\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{\tau}\odot\mathbf{f}^{(t-\tau)}\right),$
| | (3)

where $\mathbf{w}_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ restricts each past activation to its own decoder direction. For each lag, $\mathbf{w}_{\tau}$ is fit for 10 epochs with an $L_{2}$ penalty, and we report on held-out data

| | $R^{2}_{\mathrm{improve}}=1-\Big({\sum_{t}\lVert\mathbf{x}^{(t)}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{ctx}}\rVert_{2}^{2}}\Big)\Big/\Big({\sum_{t}\lVert\mathbf{x}^{(t)}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}\rVert_{2}^{2}}\Big).$
| | (4)

In the control, $\mathbf{w}_{\tau}$ is refit on past activations from the shuffled corpus with the same natural-document hidden states as targets (details in Section D.1).

Natural-document history recovers a fraction of the baseline reconstruction error that decreases with lag; shuffled history does not (Figure 1 (c)). Fitted weights at $\tau=1$ are mostly positive for natural documents and centred near zero for the shuffled control (Figure 1 (d)).

Lubana et al. [11] report that hidden-state correlations vary across a sequence and that past hidden states explain much of the current hidden state; the measurements above instead concern individual SAE features, whose persistence profiles and reconstruction contributions differ widely across the dictionary.

## 4 Persistent Sparse Autoencoders

Persistent SAEs separate a token-wise sparse activation from a persistent state (Figure 2).

Figure 2:
Persistent Sparse Autoencoders. Each feature integrates its token-wise sparse activation $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ into a persistent state $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ with its learned persistence coefficient $\lambda_{j}$ .

A BatchTopK encoder (Section B.2) produces the token-wise sparse activation $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}$ . Each feature integrates it into a persistent state $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}$ with a learned coefficient $\lambda_{j}\in[0,1]$ :

| | $h^{(t)}_{j}=\lambda_{j}h^{(t-1)}_{j}+(1-\lambda_{j})a^{(t)}_{j}.$
| | (5)

We set $\mathbf{h}^{(0)}=\mathbf{0}$ at the start of every input sequence and parameterise $\lambda_{j}=\lambda_{\max}\sigma(l_{j})$ with unconstrained $l_{j}$ and $\lambda_{\max}=0.999$ (Section B.3).

The decoder reconstructs from the persistent state:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{h}^{(t)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}.$
| | (6)

The recurrence is diagonal in feature space, so each $h^{(t)}_{j}$ contributes only along its own decoder column. Sparsity is imposed on $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ ; $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ is not constrained to be sparse. The coefficients $l_{j}$ receive gradients only from the reconstruction loss through Equations 5 and 6, with no feature partition or auxiliary temporal objective.

## 5 Experiments

We evaluate reconstruction and token-wise interpretability (Sections 5.1 and 5.2), the content of slow-feature states (Section 5.3), and long-context prompt-injection monitoring (Section 5.4).

Models and hyperparameters. 
Models and data follow Section 3. Baselines are BatchTopK SAE [8], Matryoshka SAE [9], and Temporal SAE [10].
All SAEs use $m=16{,}384$ features and a BatchTopK budget of $k=20$ ; Matryoshka and Temporal SAEs share the same predefined 20%/80% feature partition. Full configuration is in Appendix B.

### 5.1 Reconstruction Quality and Learned Timescales

The learned coefficients span a broad range, with most features at short timescales and a small long-timescale tail (Figure 3 (a)).
We define slow features as the highest $1\%$ by $\lambda_{j}$ and fast features as the lowest $50\%$ .

We report fraction of variance explained (FVE), cosine similarity between hidden state and reconstruction, fraction of alive features, and the temporal smoothness metric of Bhalla et al. [10]. Persistent SAEs remain competitive with the strongest baselines in reconstruction (Table 1): FVE 0.93 versus 0.94 for BatchTopK on Pythia and 0.66 versus 0.72 on Gemma. Slow-feature smoothness is 0.05 on Pythia and 0.04 on Gemma, against at least 0.12 for every baseline group; fast features score 0.20 on both models.

Grouping features into $\lambda_{j}$ quintiles, median $R_{j}(\tau)$ is ordered by quintile across lags on both models, with higher- $\lambda_{j}$ groups decaying more slowly (Figure 3 (b)); the Temporal SAE’s predefined high-level and low-level groups are not clearly separated by $R_{j}(\tau)$ .

### 5.2 Short-Timescale Features Are Locally Interpretable

We use the automated interpretability pipeline of Bills et al. [23]: a judge model explains a feature from its highest-activation contexts and is scored on how well the explanation predicts activation. For the Persistent SAE, the scored quantity is $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ rather than $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ (Appendix E).

Fast features score 0.93 on Pythia and 0.89 on Gemma, matching or exceeding the best baseline on each model; slow features score 0.84 and 0.79 (Table 1, right).
In qualitative examples (Tables 4 and 5, Appendix E), fast features respond to compact lexical or grammatical patterns such as letters or substrings, with activation concentrated at the current token; slow features more often correspond to broad subjects or contextual conditions with activation distributed across the sequence.
Token-specific explanation protocols are known to assign similar descriptions to distinct features [24] and to produce explanations that fail to generalise to related inputs [25]; Section 5.3 therefore evaluates slow features jointly.

Where Features Receive New Evidence. 
We divide features into five equal-sized $\lambda$ quintiles and assign their update positions to six token categories: punctuation, conjunctions, function words, verbs, adjectives or adverbs, and nouns, following the lexical/function-word distinction [26].
Function words (Func. in Figure 4) include adpositions, determiners, particles, and pronouns.
For quintile $q$ and category $c$ ,

| | $U_{q,c}={\Pr\!\left(T^{(t)}=c\mid a^{(t)}_{j}>0,\;j\in Q_{q}\right)}\big/{\Pr\!\left(T^{(t)}=c\right)},$
| | (7)

where $T^{(t)}$ is the category of token $t$ and $Q_{q}$ the set of features in quintile $q$ .

Figure 4: Relative update frequency $U_{q,c}$ by $\lambda$ -quintile and token category. Orange and blue indicate values above and below one.

The lowest- $\lambda$ quintile is updated disproportionately at nouns; the highest- $\lambda$ quintile at punctuation and conjunctions (Figure 4).
Punctuation and other function-like tokens carry substantial contextual information in LLMs [27], and explicit structural markers gate cross-sentence integration
[28].
Autointerpretations of high- $\lambda$ features frequently describe broad semantic domains (Tables 4 and 5).

### 5.3 Long-Timescale States Track Subject Information

Slow features form subject-specific clusters. 
We embed MMLU [29] examples from five subjects with t-SNE, using the final $20$ token representations of each sample (Appendix F) and, for the Persistent SAE, the highest $1\%$ of features by $\lambda_{j}$ . BatchTopK features mix subjects heavily and the Temporal SAE’s predefined high-level group separates them only partially, whereas the slow Persistent SAE state forms coherent subject regions, more clearly separated than raw hidden states (Figure 5). No subject labels enter Persistent SAE training.

Temporal Persistence Selects Subject-Informative Features Without Labels. 
On spliced MMLU sequences, built by concatenating labelled segments from different subjects so that the subject changes at segment boundaries, a per-token linear probe predicts the current subject from a varying fraction of the dictionary. Persistent SAE features are ranked by decreasing $\lambda_{j}$ , increasing $\lambda_{j}$ , or randomly; we also compare BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and Temporal SAE representations and a supervised oracle ranking that, per subject, favours features more strongly active on that subject than on all others (Appendix G).

Selection by decreasing $\lambda_{j}$ nearly matches the supervised oracle (Figure 6). On both models the slowest $1\%$ of features reach high AUC, while low- $\lambda_{j}$ , random, and baseline SAE representations retain substantially less subject information at the same budget.

### 5.4 Case Study: Persistent Prompt Injection Monitoring

In indirect prompt injection [12], an agent encounters a malicious instruction in an email, webpage, or tool response, continues reasoning for hundreds of tokens, and acts later [30]; an agentic monitor must retain a security-relevant signal until the action [31, 32].

Setting. 
We use AgentDojo trajectories from the banking, travel, and workspace domains [12], generated by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct [33] (Section C.3). Each trajectory contains a request, an untrusted span holding a prompt injection or benign content, and the agent’s subsequent tool calls. We retain only failed attacks, in which an injection is present but the agent does not complete the attack’s action.

Gemma-2-2B serves as an external monitor: each trajectory is replayed and the layer-12 residual stream recorded. A linear probe is trained at the final token of the untrusted span ( $d=0$ ) and evaluated without retraining up to $350$ tokens later (Figure 7 (a)). We compare the raw hidden state and baseline SAE representations with the Persistent SAE state $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ restricted to slow features (highest $1\%$ by $\lambda_{j}$ ) or fast features (lowest $50\%$ ), as in Section 5.1 (Appendix H).

Figure 7:
Persistent monitoring of prompt injection. (a) A probe trained at the end of an untrusted span is evaluated later in the trajectory. (b) Probe accuracy across distance (top) and causal effect on the monitor’s judgement (bottom).

Signal retention: fast features detect local injections while slow states retain signals over long contexts. 
At $d=0$ , the fast-feature state and standard SAE representations give the strongest detection (Figure 7 (b), top); with increasing distance from the untrusted span their accuracy falls towards chance, while the slow-feature state retains a clearer signal at longer distances.

Causal effect: slow-feature directions causally influence the monitor’s judgement. 
We truncate each trajectory at a later distance, append a query asking whether it should be flagged for prompt injection, and intervene at the final query token.
Following work that selects SAE features for steering and uses linear classifiers to identify task-relevant sparse subspaces [7, 34], we build for each SAE representation $r$ a steering vector $\mathbf{v}_{r}$ from its most predictive decoder directions weighted by probe coefficients, and apply it with both signs. With $s(\mathbf{x})=\ell_{\mathrm{yes}}(\mathbf{x})-\ell_{\mathrm{no}}(\mathbf{x})$ the monitor’s logit margin,

| | $\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{causal}}(r,d)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{i}\Big[s\big(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(d)}+\alpha_{i}^{(d)}\mathbf{v}_{r}\big)-s\big(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(d)}-\alpha_{i}^{(d)}\mathbf{v}_{r}\big)\Big],$
| | (8)

where $\alpha_{i}^{(d)}$ scales each intervention to $10\%$ of the hidden-state norm.

Slow-feature directions give the largest and consistently positive $\Delta_{\mathrm{causal}}$ at every distance. Directions built from BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and Temporal SAE features give near-zero or negative effects, with no comparable alignment over distance. Fast features thus supply local detection, and the slow state supplies an injection-related signal that remains both decodable and aligned with the monitor’s judgement long after the injected span.

## 6 Conclusion and Discussion

Conclusion. 
Persistent SAEs learn per-feature persistence coefficients from reconstruction alone. The coefficients span a broad range: low- $\lambda_{j}$ features remain locally interpretable, and high- $\lambda_{j}$ states track subject identity and preserve monitoring signals over long contexts, yielding an unsupervised organisation of sparse representations by timescale.

Limitations and Future Work. 
Each feature has a single fixed coefficient under a diagonal recurrence, which excludes interactions between features and context-dependent resets. The prompt-injection study uses an external replay monitor, so interventions establish effects on the monitor’s judgement rather than on the original agent’s actions. Richer recurrent dynamics and end-to-end tests of persistent feature interventions on agent behaviour remain open.
