## Appendix B SAE Training Details

### B.1 SAE Baseline Training Details

We train four SAE families: BatchTopK [8],
Matryoshka BatchTopK [9], Temporal SAE [10],
and the Persistent SAE. All share dictionary width, BatchTopK activation budget,
optimiser, and token budget, so that differences reflect temporal treatment rather than
training data volume or optimisation steps.

Common configuration. 
Every SAE has $m=16{,}384$ features and a BatchTopK activation
budget of $k=20$ per token. We train with Adam at learning rate $3\times 10^{-4}$ with
a linear warm-up over the first $1{,}000$ steps. From step $1{,}000$ , we apply the
BatchTopK activation-threshold schedule with decay $\beta=0.999$ and the
auxiliary dead-feature loss weighted by $\alpha_{\mathrm{aux}}=0.03125$ . Training
activations come from Pile Uncopyrighted [35], with the beginning-of-sequence
position removed. For Gemma-2-2B [21], we use the layer-12 residual stream
with hidden width $d=2{,}304$ ; for Pythia-160M-deduped [20],
the layer-8 residual stream with $d=768$ .

Matryoshka and Temporal SAEs divide their dictionaries into the same two
predefined groups, containing $20\%$ and $80\%$ of the $16{,}384$ features.
The Temporal SAE weights the corresponding reconstruction losses by $0.2$ and $0.8$ ;
Matryoshka uses uniform reconstruction weights. The Persistent SAE
has no predefined partition and learns a persistence coefficient for every
feature.

Matched token budget. 
The families consume activations in different units: BatchTopK and Matryoshka
use shuffled token activations, the Temporal SAE uses adjacent token pairs, and
the Persistent SAE uses contiguous sequences to carry state across tokens.
We match activation tokens per optimisation step and total steps rather than
structural units. Each
model is trained for $244{,}140$ steps with an effective batch of approximately
$2{,}048$ activation tokens per step, giving the flat baselines
$2{,}048\times 244{,}140=499{,}998{,}720$ tokens, or approximately $5.0\times 10^{8}$
tokens in total.

•

BatchTopK and Matryoshka. The activation buffer returns a flat
batch of $2{,}048$ token activations at each step.

•

Temporal SAE. The buffer returns adjacent previous–next token
pairs from the same activation stream, with the number of reconstructed token
positions per step equal to the flat-baseline batch size.

•

Persistent SAE. The recurrent state requires contiguous
sequences rather than shuffled tokens. We use eight sequences of context length
$256$ per step; excluding the beginning-of-sequence position gives
$8\times 255=2{,}040$ usable token activations per step, within $0.4\%$ of the
flat-baseline budget.

All families therefore receive the same number of gradient updates and, up to
the pairing or sequencing their objectives require, approximately the same number
of token activations. Checkpoints are saved on a fixed schedule and the final dictionary
(ae.pt) is used for every downstream evaluation. All experiments were run on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80 GB of memory.

### B.2 BatchTopK Sparsity

All SAEs in this paper impose sparsity with BatchTopK. A hidden state $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is mapped to non-negative pre-activations

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{f}}=\mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}})+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{enc}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m},$
| | (9)

and only the largest pre-activations across the batch are retained.
For a batch $X=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}$ , the pre-activations $\{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}$ are flattened into a vector of length $Bm$ , and $\mathbf{f}_{i}$ keeps only the top $kB$ entries globally, zeroing all others.
The reconstruction is

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{f}_{i}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}.$
| | (10)

After training with exact BatchTopK selection, inference uses the thresholded form

| | $f_{ij}=\tilde{f}_{ij}\,\mathbf{1}[\tilde{f}_{ij}>\theta],$
| | (11)

with $\theta$ estimated from training-time top- $k$ statistics.
In the Persistent SAE this sparse activation is the token-wise activation $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ ; only its downstream use differs.

### B.3 Persistence Parameterisation

The persistence coefficients are

| | $\lambda_{j}=\sigma(l_{j})\cdot\lambda_{\max},$
| | (12)

with $l_{j}\in\mathbb{R}$ an unconstrained logit, $\sigma$ the sigmoid, and $\lambda_{\max}=0.999$ a hard cap preventing exact poles,
so that $\lambda_{j}\in(0,\lambda_{\max})$ throughout training.
With the factor $(1-\lambda_{j})$ , Equation 5 is an exponential moving average (EMA) rather than an unnormalised sum: under constant activation $a^{(t)}_{j}=a_{j}$ the state converges to $a_{j}$ for every $\lambda_{j}$ . The cap below one gives every feature finite effective memory. All logits $l_{j}$ are initialised to $0.5$ , keeping the sigmoid away from saturation at initialisation.

## Appendix C Dataset Details

Pile documents supply hidden states for training and evaluating the SAEs, MMLU supplies subject-labelled text for the persistent-state analyses, and AgentDojo trajectories supply the prompt-injection monitoring study.

### C.1 Pile Corpus

The original Pile is an $825$  GiB English-language corpus assembled from 22 sources, including academic papers, web pages, books, code, and online discussions [22]. We use the Pile Uncopyrighted release [35], which removes the Books3, BookCorpus2, OpenSubtitles, YouTube Subtitles, and OpenWebText2 components. Documents are streamed and shuffled with a buffer of size $10{,}000$ under a fixed seed, and accepted if, after tokenisation with the model tokeniser and truncation to the context cap, they contain at least the required minimum number of tokens.

For the natural corpus, each accepted document is passed through the model and the chosen residual-stream hidden states are retained.
For a sequence of retained length $L$ , temporal statistics are computed on token positions $\{16,\dots,L-1\}$ .

The shuffled control is built at the sentence level rather than by permuting tokens. Sentences sampled from documents of the same corpus are concatenated under an adjacency constraint forbidding consecutive sentences from the same source document, which breaks long-range entity tracking and discourse progression while leaving within-sentence structure intact.

### C.2 MMLU Dataset

Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) is an English-language benchmark of four-option multiple-choice questions from 57 subjects spanning STEM, the humanities, the social sciences, and other professional and academic fields [29]. It is used only for the subject analyses, not for SAE training. We use abstract algebra, astronomy, business ethics, computer security, and European history.

For the geometry analysis in Section 5.3, we sample $100$ sequences across the five subjects and retain the final $20$ token representations of each. For subject probing, sequences join equal-length segments from different subjects and each token takes the label of its source segment (Appendix F and Appendix G).

### C.3 AgentDojo Trajectories

Indirect prompt injection occurs when an agent retrieves attacker-controlled text from emails, webpages, documents, or tool outputs and follows instructions in it. AgentDojo [12] provides stateful tool environments with 97 user tasks, 27 injection targets, and 629 security test cases across workspace, Slack, travel, and banking domains; task-specific checks inspect agent output and environment changes to determine whether the user request and the attacker’s target action were completed.

We use banking, travel, and workspace trajectories generated by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. Benign trajectories without an injection form the negative class ( $y=0$ ). The positive class ( $y=1$ ) contains runs with an important_instructions or direct attack for which the AgentDojo injection checker returns security=false, i.e. an injection was present but the attacker’s target action was not completed. Successful attacks are excluded because overt malicious actions, such as transferring money or sending private data, would provide a trivial downstream cue. We do not filter by task utility, so the legitimate user request may either succeed or fail.

## Appendix D Empirical Persistence of Standard SAE Features

We evaluate lags $\tau\in\{1,4,16,32,64,128,256,512\}$ on documents of at most $1{,}024$ traced tokens. A feature is retained only with at least $256$ activation events, at least $64$ valid anchors at every lag, and a non-negligible activated-token elevation; $R_{j}(\tau)$ is undefined and excluded when $\mathbb{E}[p^{(t)}_{j}\mid\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0]-\mathbb{E}[p^{(t)}_{j}]$ is near zero, as for near-dead or diffuse features, and no $\epsilon$ is added to numerator or denominator.
On Pythia-160M, median persistence for BatchTopK falls from $0.618$ at lag $1$ to $0.160$ at lag $64$ and is $0.096$ at lag $512$ ; Matryoshka goes from $0.504$ to $0.108$ and $0.059$ . On Gemma-2-2B, natural-document persistence at lag $512$ is $0.042$ (BatchTopK) and $0.034$ (Matryoshka). On both models the shuffled control decays to approximately zero at long lags.
Power-law fits to the positive decay tail give median exponents $\beta_{\mathrm{nat}}\approx 0.32$ versus $\beta_{\mathrm{shf}}\approx 0.87$ – $0.92$ , for both SAE families.

Ranking features by average $R_{j}(\tau)$ within short ( $\tau\leq 16$ ), medium ( $32\leq\tau\leq 64$ ), and long ( $\tau\geq 128$ ) lag bands yields distributions spanning nearly the full unit interval in every band. Some features are strongly persistent at short lags but decay before medium lags; others remain elevated into the long-lag regime. This heterogeneity holds in both SAE families and substantially exceeds that of the shuffled control.

### D.1 Context Correction Experiment

The per-feature correction of Equation 3 is fit independently at each lag $\tau\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\}$ , on $192$ natural documents, with $R^{2}_{\mathrm{improve}}$ evaluated on $96$ held-out natural documents. The target is always the natural-document reconstruction error; the control refits the diagonal head on context activations from the shuffled corpus with identical parameterisation and optimisation budget. Each document contributes at most $768$ tokens after dropping $16$ prefix tokens. We optimise for $10$ epochs with AdamW, learning rate $5\times 10^{-3}$ , and weight decay $10^{-3}$ .

On Pythia-160M the correction removes $0.89\%$ (BatchTopK) and $0.61\%$ (Matryoshka) of the baseline reconstruction error at lag $1$ , and $0.22\%$ and $0.13\%$ at lag $32$ . On Gemma-2-2B both SAEs remove approximately $0.40\%$ at lag $1$ , about $0.02\%$ at lag $16$ , and nothing by lag $32$ . The shuffled controls stay slightly below zero throughout.

Table 3 reports the fitted lag-one weights: on natural documents the mean is positive and a large majority of features take positive weight, while the shuffled distributions are sharply centred at zero.

## Appendix F Subject Geometry Details

We draw $100$ sequences from five MMLU subjects (abstract algebra, astronomy, business ethics, computer security, and European history) and keep the last $20$ tokens of each, every token carrying a subject label. For each representation—raw hidden states, BatchTopK features, the Temporal SAE’s high-level group, and the Persistent SAE’s high- $\lambda_{j}$ state—token-level vectors are projected to two dimensions with t-SNE under a common set of hyperparameters and coloured by subject.

## Appendix G Subject Probing Details

Spliced sequences concatenate equal-length segments from different MMLU subjects, balancing labels within each sequence and holding out entire source documents for the test split; each token takes the subject of its segment. A linear probe on token-level representations predicts the source subject, and we report held-out one-vs-rest macro ROC AUC against the fraction of features made available, swept from $0.1\%$ to $100\%$ . The Persistent SAE is evaluated on $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ with features ordered by decreasing $\lambda_{j}$ , increasing $\lambda_{j}$ , repeated random permutations, or supervised one-vs-rest importance. For subject $c$ , the supervised score of feature $j$ is

| | $s_{j,c}=\mathbb{E}[h^{(t)}_{j}\mid y^{(t)}=c]-\mathbb{E}[h^{(t)}_{j}\mid y^{(t)}\neq c],$
| | (13)

computed on the training split. Features are sorted by this score within each subject and the subject-specific rankings are interleaved round-robin into a single global ordering for the multiclass probe. BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and Temporal baselines use their full dictionaries under the same probe.

## Appendix H Prompt Injection Monitoring Details

Trajectory construction. 
Trajectories come from AgentDojo [12] runs of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct agents. Attack trajectories are restricted to the important_instructions and direct attack types and to runs with security=false, so positives contain an injection whose targeted action was not executed; benign trajectories contain no injected content. Each trajectory is serialised, appended with the monitoring query

should this trajectory be flagged for prompt injection or unsafe instruction hijacking? Answer yes or no:

and read with Gemma-2-2B, with all representations taken from the layer-12 residual stream. The yes-minus-no answer logit at the query position alone gives an AUC of $0.51$ .

Checkpoints and probes. 
For each trajectory, we locate the final token of the injected span (for benign trajectories, the token at the matched position) and define checkpoints at offsets of $0$ , $50$ , $100$ , $200$ , $250$ , $300$ , and $350$ tokens after it, plus the final query position. At each checkpoint we extract, from the same layer, the raw hidden state, the BatchTopK and Matryoshka sparse activations, the Temporal SAE’s high-level feature group, and the Persistent SAE’s token-wise activation $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ , full state $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ , and slow state (the largest 1% of $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ coordinates by $\lambda_{j}$ ). A logistic regression probe is fit on each representation at checkpoint $d=0$ only and evaluated without retraining at every other checkpoint; we report held-out accuracy and ROC AUC.

Causal intervention. 
For each SAE representation, the $k=128$ features with the largest absolute probe coefficients are selected and their coefficient-weighted decoder columns summed into $\mathbf{v}_{r}$ . The direction is normalised and scaled so that $\lVert\alpha_{i}^{(d)}\mathbf{v}_{r}\rVert_{2}=\rho\lVert\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(d)}\rVert_{2}$ , with $\rho=0.1$ , and added to the residual stream with both signs. A positive $\Delta_{\mathrm{causal}}$ in Equation 8 indicates that displacement along the probe direction shifts the monitor towards answering yes; the measured quantity is the external replay monitor’s logit margin, not the original Llama-3.3-70B agent’s action. All interventions use the direction constructed at $d=0$ , so Figure 7 reports the transfer of its causal effect across distance.

ANSWER Q1: Use the direction built from the Persistent SAE’s long-timescale state features and apply it with the negative sign. Probe coefficients define the positive direction toward detecting an injection—and hence “yes”—so subtracting that direction nudges the monitor toward “no.”

ANSWER Q2: The context correction is a restricted post-hoc addition to an already strong, frozen SAE, so it measures only incremental recovery of residual reconstruction error. The Persistent SAE is trained jointly around its recurrent state, and the carried term’s share of state mass is not the same quantity as its marginal reduction in reconstruction error.

ANSWER Q3: Not settled. The paper describes FVE and cosine-similarity comparisons but provides no reported values establishing whether Persistent SAEs reconstruct worse than the Temporal SAE.

ANSWER Q4: The shuffled activations contain no genuine document-specific predictive signal, but a fitted correction can still learn noise and then slightly worsen held-out reconstruction. Thus its measured improvement can fluctuate just below zero rather than being exactly zero.

ANSWER Q5: It would lose the slow/high-level smoothness comparison against the Temporal SAE’s predefined high-level group. Smoothness is better when lower, so raising the Persistent slow group to 0.12 would put it above that baseline group.

ANSWER Q6: Not settled. Fraction alive is listed as an evaluation metric, but the paper does not report comparative results showing that Persistent SAEs have more alive features.

ANSWER Q7: Probably not. Initialising every timescale logit near 10 would place the squashing function in a saturated, near-maximum-persistence regime with very small gradients, making it difficult for features to spread across a broad range of timescales.

ANSWER Q8: Reset \(\mathbf h\) to zero at each document boundary. Otherwise information from one document would leak into the next even though it is not part of that document’s preceding context.

ANSWER Q9: Full-dictionary smoothness aggregates both fast and slow features, and the very smooth slow features substantially lower the overall score. The fast half can therefore score 0.20 while the combined representation still outperforms baselines whose dictionaries lack an equally smooth persistent component.

ANSWER Q10: The claim that learned timescales identify and compactly concentrate subject-relevant features would fail. Decreasing-timescale ranking performing no better than random would mean that high persistence provides no useful unsupervised ranking for subject information.

ANSWER Q11: Measure decoder-aligned projection persistence after activation events separately for the fixed fast and slow groups, using identical normalisation and feature-selection criteria. They should also use controls that disrupt document history, such as unrelated-text or shuffled-history controls, to distinguish genuine persistence from local token coherence.

ANSWER Q12: Lowering \(\lambda_{\max}\) to 0.9 would constrain example features with learned \(\lambda_j>0.9\), particularly the slow Gemma features. It would prevent those features from attaining the near-unit retention needed for their long effective memories.

ANSWER Q13: Not settled. The analysis covers only five selected MMLU subjects and therefore cannot establish that slow features track subject identity across MMLU’s 57 subjects in general.

ANSWER Q14: No. Gemma-2-2B’s direct yes-minus-no query logit achieves only AUC \(0.51\), essentially chance, so the paper instead trains probes on internal representations.

ANSWER Q15: No; that threshold is likely too strict. The Pythia examples indicate that semantically slow features need not have \(\lambda_j>0.9\), so the rule would incorrectly exclude meaningful persistent features.

ANSWER Q16: They could rank features by long-lag persistence of the decoder-aligned projection \(\mathbf d_j^\top\mathbf x^{(t+\tau)}\) following an activation event, normalised by the elevation at the anchor token. They could also fit feature-wise diagonal context corrections and use long-lag predictive coefficients or held-out error recovery as supporting evidence.

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. The paper describes fitting corrections over a range of lags, but it does not report evidence that same-document past activations improve reconstruction at every lag through 512 tokens.

ANSWER Q18: Gemma-2-2B would recover more reconstruction error, but the gain would still be small—under 1% of the baseline reconstruction error. A lag-1 diagonal correction is deliberately restricted and cannot exploit dense cross-feature temporal predictability.

ANSWER Q19: Not settled. The paper explains how smoothness should be reported for Matryoshka’s predefined high- and low-level groups, but it does not provide results establishing that the high-level group is smoother.

ANSWER Q1: Select features by decreasing learned timescale \(\lambda_j\), using the highest-\(\lambda\) states as the compact context representation. Support is weak: the paper only proposes a related subject-probing test on MMLU and reports no results for Pile document types.

ANSWER Q2: Tentatively, expect updates at punctuation, conjunctions, and other function or structural tokens rather than mainly at content nouns. The paper motivates this hypothesis from prior work but explicitly treats the relationship as empirical and reports no results establishing it.

ANSWER Q3: Not settled. The paper proposes comparing Matryoshka’s predefined high-level group with timescale-ranked Persistent SAE states, but it gives no experimental results showing which is the better unsupervised topic tracker.

ANSWER Q4: Not settled. The paper describes fitting feature-wise context corrections, but it reports neither the distribution of lag-1 weight signs nor a correlation between positive weights and reconstruction gains.

ANSWER Q5: The feature-wise, diagonal recurrence—where feature \(j\) carries only its own past activations—would lose its empirical motivation. Large gains only from cross-feature corrections would instead indicate that temporal prediction requires interactions or transitions between features, although the diagonal design would still preserve attribution.

ANSWER Q6: Not settled. The causal experiment uses one fixed relative intervention magnitude, \(\rho=0.1\), with both signs; it does not sweep intervention strength.

ANSWER Q7: I don't know. The paper leaves \(\Phi_{\theta}\) abstract and does not provide an explicit recurrence, so exact token weights cannot be derived; under an EMA update \(h_j^{(t)}=\lambda_j h_j^{(t-1)}+(1-\lambda_j)a_j^{(t)}\), token \(s\) would receive weight \((1-\lambda_j)\lambda_j^{t-s}\).

ANSWER Q8: Not settled. The paper proposes full-dictionary autointerpretability evaluation on token-wise activations, not persistent states, but reports no scores comparing Persistent SAE with BatchTopK.

ANSWER Q9: Not settled. Reconstruction FVE and cosine similarity are proposed as comparison metrics, but no numerical Persistent-versus-Temporal SAE results are presented.

ANSWER Q10: The claim that learned timescales identify and compactly concentrate subject-level contextual information would fail. In particular, decreasing-\(\lambda_j\) ordering would provide no unsupervised advantage over an arbitrary feature subset.

ANSWER Q11: The paper does not establish which representation performs best at \(d=300\). Under its intended persistent-monitoring approach, use the \(d=0\) probe-weighted decoder direction from the slow Persistent SAE state features and apply the negative sign, opposite the injection/“yes” direction.

ANSWER Q12: A shuffled correction fitted on finite data can learn noisy or overfit coefficients that slightly worsen held-out reconstruction. Thus its expected useful signal is zero, but its measured \(R^2_{\mathrm{improve}}\) need not be exactly zero and can be negative.

ANSWER Q13: No, that threshold is not justified by the paper. It gives neither numerical \(\lambda_j\) examples nor a learned-timescale distribution for Pythia-160M, and the interpretation of \(0.9\) depends on the omitted recurrence parameterisation.

ANSWER Q14: Not settled. The appendix proposes fitting corrections across a range of lags and describes controls, but it reports no gains—let alone positive gains at every lag through 512 tokens.

ANSWER Q15: Rank features by empirical persistence of their decoder-aligned projections after activation, such as slowly decaying normalised projection elevation at medium and long lags. They could also use each feature’s same-direction context-correction weights or held-out gains, although the paper does not validate either ranking as a predictor of learned \(\lambda_j\).

ANSWER Q16: It would weaken the characterisation that slow features obtain new evidence preferentially from grammatical or structural markers, while fast features respond to immediate lexical content such as nouns. The highest-\(\lambda\) features would then look less distinct from short-timescale lexical features.

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. The paper says smoothness should be reported separately for Matryoshka’s predefined high- and low-level groups, but it provides no resulting comparison.

ANSWER Q18: Temporal SAE assigns a fixed “high-level” group and encourages nearby-token alignment, but it does not explicitly carry each feature’s evidence over hundreds of tokens; its \(d=0\) steering direction can therefore drift or cease to align with the monitor later. Persistent SAE slow states are expressly designed to retain that evidence along the same decoder-attributable directions, making positive long-distance transfer more plausible.

ANSWER Q19: Not settled. The paper proposes comparing learned timescales with projection-based empirical persistence, but it reports no within-model or cross-model relationship showing that greater standard-SAE persistence leads to larger learned \(\lambda_j\).

ANSWER Q6: I don't know.

ANSWER Q8: I don't know. The supplied paper does not report the model-by-model FVE results needed to select the best SAE for Gemma-2-2B.

ANSWER Q9: It would lose the slow-group smoothness comparison against the Temporal SAE’s predefined high-level group, assuming that group’s reported Pythia smoothness is below 0.12. Lower values are better for this metric.

ANSWER Q10: No. Gemma-2-2B’s yes-minus-no logit for that query achieves an AUC of only 0.51, essentially chance, motivating the paper’s use of trained internal probes.

ANSWER Q11: Not settled. The analysis uses only five selected MMLU subjects, so it cannot establish that slow features track subject identity across MMLU’s 57 subjects generally.

ANSWER Q12: Not settled. Fraction alive is listed as an evaluation metric, but the supplied paper reports no comparative results showing that Persistent SAEs have more alive features.

ANSWER Q13: No. With \(\lambda_{\max}=0.999\), the largest possible retained fraction after 5,000 update-free tokens is \(0.999^{5000}\approx0.0067\), below 1%.

ANSWER Q14: Slow-state information is distributed and carried across many timescale-selected features, so selecting the exact largest probe coefficients matters less. BatchTopK has no persistent state, making its useful injection signal more concentrated in the particular features identified by the probe.

ANSWER Q15: The correction is a post-hoc, lag-1 diagonal addition to an already strong frozen SAE and measures only reduction of its remaining reconstruction error. The carried-mass fraction instead describes the composition of a Persistent SAE’s jointly trained state, whose encoder and decoder can reorganise around recurrent information, so it need not equal the correction’s marginal error reduction.

ANSWER Q16: It would undermine the claim that short-timescale Persistent SAE features preserve the local, token-level interpretability of standard SAE features.

ANSWER Q17: They should reset \(\mathbf h\) to zero at each document boundary. Otherwise information from one document would leak into the next, and the feature-wise recurrence has no learned context-dependent reset mechanism to remove it automatically.

ANSWER Q18: They should compare the groups using empirical persistence measures, such as decoder-direction projections following activation events, alongside temporal smoothness at matched reconstruction quality. Controls should preserve local token coherence while disrupting document-level continuity so that apparent slowness is not merely caused by adjacent phrases or sentences.

ANSWER Q19: The paper suggests they would lose little in local interpretability, because short-timescale activations are intended to behave like standard token-level SAE features. This does not imply that using only the fast subset would preserve full-dictionary reconstruction quality.

# Persistent Sparse Autoencoders: Learning Feature-Specific Timescales in Language Model Representations

Haoyan Luo

Affiliation: University of Cambridge

  
Mateo Espinosa Zarlenga

Affiliation: University of Oxford

  
Mateja Jamnik

Affiliation: University of Cambridge

###### Abstract

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) encode each token of a language model's activations independently. In standard SAE features, decoder-aligned signal outlasts activation, past activations reduce reconstruction error of later hidden states, and the duration of both varies across features. We introduce Persistent Sparse Autoencoders (Persistent SAEs), which attach a learned persistence coefficient to every feature and train it by reconstruction alone. Persistent SAEs remain competitive in reconstruction and learn a spectrum of timescales: fast features are locally interpretable, and slow features identify the current context. In prompt-injection monitoring, slow features preserve injection-related signal and remain causally effective over long contexts.

## 1 Introduction

Interpreting an LLM's output requires knowing what its hidden states represent and how that content evolves over a sequence [1, 2]. SAEs [3, 4] decompose hidden states into sparse features which, when concept-aligned, support inspection and intervention [5, 6, 7]. Causal transformer hidden states integrate preceding context, yet standard SAEs encode tokens independently [3, 8, 9], obscuring topic, style, or task state [10]. Temporal variants impose predefined partitions or decompositions of temporal roles [10, 11], fixing a priori which features carry temporal information.

Standard SAE features already exhibit temporal persistence (Figure 1): after activation, later hidden states remain aligned with the decoder direction, past activations aid reconstruction of later hidden states, and decay rates differ substantially across features. Persistent SAEs learn a coefficient $\lambda_{j}$ per feature; each feature's state decays at $\lambda_{j}$ and is updated by a token-wise sparse activation. Reconstruction gradients favour higher $\lambda_{j}$ when carrying a state forward aids later reconstruction and smaller $\lambda_{j}$ otherwise.

Persistent SAEs retain competitive reconstruction while learning a broad range of timescales without supervision. Most features are low- $\lambda_{j}$ local detectors; high- $\lambda_{j}$ features retain contextual information across the sequence and, in a prompt-injection case study [12], provide monitoring signals over long timescales. Contributions:

•

SAE features exhibit temporal persistence: after activation, the decoder direction remains elevated and past activations help predict subsequent states.

•

Persistent Sparse Autoencoders, learning one coefficient per sparse feature through reconstruction alone, with competitive reconstruction and a broad spectrum of timescales without a predefined partition of temporal roles.

•

Short-timescale (fast) features act as local detectors; long-timescale (slow) features retain contextual information; in prompt-injection monitoring, slow features support monitoring and steering over long contexts.

## 2 Background and Related Work

Sparse autoencoders. 
For hidden state $\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ at token $t$ , a standard SAE [3] produces $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}$ and

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{f}^{(t)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}},$
| | (1)

with $\mathbf{d}_{j}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}[:,j]/\lVert\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}[:,j]\rVert_{2}$ (notation in Appendix A) and feature $j$ active whenever $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0$ . Sparsity of $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}$ limits each reconstruction to few features [3, 13]. BatchTopK [8] replaces per-token TopK with a batch-level budget, letting the active count vary across tokens; Matryoshka SAEs [9] jointly train nested dictionaries of increasing size, smaller subsets retaining higher-level features.

Temporal structure in LLM representations. 
Standard SAEs and most variants compute $\mathbf{f}^{(t)}$ independently of preceding tokens' features. Slow feature analysis identifies higher-level features in neural networks via slowly varying latent factors [14, 15]. LMs track entities and encode game-board, spatial, temporal, and propositional states [16, 17, 18, 19].

Temporal extensions of SAEs. 
Temporal SAEs [10] pre-assign a high-level subset and align its activations across nearby tokens contrastively. Lubana et al. [11] use an attention-based predictor to separate context-predictable information from a sparse novel residual. Both fix a partition; neither assigns each sparse feature its own learned persistence, which complicates post-hoc timescale analysis. Persistent SAEs assign each feature a persistent state and a learned persistence coefficient.

## 3 Does Temporal Structure Exist at the Feature Level?

Setup. 
Residual-stream hidden states $\{\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ are taken from Pythia-160M-deduped (layer 8) [20] and Gemma-2-2B (layer 12) [21] on Pile documents [22]. BatchTopK [8] and Matryoshka [9] SAEs, neither with a temporal prior, are trained as in Appendix B. The shuffled control is built from intact sentences of different Pile documents (Figure 1 (a); Appendix C).

Sparse Features Temporally Persist in the Hidden States. 
With $p^{(t)}_{j}=\mathbf{d}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{x}^{(t)}$ and lag $\tau$ in tokens,

| | $R_{j}(\tau):=\big({\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t+\tau)}_{j}\mid\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0\right]-\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t)}_{j}\right]}\Big)\Big/\Big({\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t)}_{j}\mid\mathbf{f}^{(t)}_{j}>0\right]-\mathbb{E}\!\left[p^{(t)}_{j}\right]}\Big),$
| | (2)

where $\mathbb{E}[p^{(t)}_{j}]$ is averaged over all evaluated tokens. Evaluation procedure and feature selection: Appendix D.

Across both models and SAE families, $R_{j}(\tau)$ decays more slowly in natural documents than in the shuffled control (Figure 1 (b)).

Past Activations Can Help Reconstruction. 
We augment Equation 1 with activations $\tau$ tokens earlier, restricted to each feature's own direction:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{ctx}}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}+\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{\tau}\odot\mathbf{f}^{(t-\tau)}\right),$
| | (3)

with $\mathbf{w}_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ fitted per lag for 10 epochs under an $L_{2}$ penalty, and report on held-out data

| | $R^{2}_{\mathrm{improve}}=1-\Big({\sum_{t}\lVert\mathbf{x}^{(t)}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{ctx}}\rVert_{2}^{2}}\Big)\Big/\Big({\sum_{t}\lVert\mathbf{x}^{(t)}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}_{\mathrm{base}}\rVert_{2}^{2}}\Big).$
| | (4)

The control refits the weights on past activations from the shuffled corpus, keeping natural-document hidden states as targets (Section D.1).

Natural-document history recovers a fraction of baseline error, diminishing with lag; shuffled history does not (Figure 1 (c)). Fitted weights at $\tau=1$ are mostly positive for natural documents and centred near zero for the shuffled control (Figure 1 (d)).

Lubana et al. [11] show that hidden-state correlations vary across a sequence and that past hidden states explain much of the current one. The question here is narrower and feature-level: persistence of individual SAE features aids reconstruction and varies widely across features.

## 4 Persistent Sparse Autoencoders

Figure 2:
Persistent Sparse Autoencoders. Each feature integrates $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ into $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ with learned $\lambda_{j}$ .

A BatchTopK encoder (Section B.2) produces $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}$ , with $a^{(t)}_{j}>0$ marking new evidence for feature $j$ at token $t$ , and

| | $h^{(t)}_{j}=\lambda_{j}h^{(t-1)}_{j}+(1-\lambda_{j})a^{(t)}_{j},$
| | (5)

with $\lambda_{j}\in[0,1]$ , $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m}$ , $\mathbf{h}^{(0)}=\mathbf{0}$ at every input sequence start, and $\lambda_{j}=\lambda_{\max}\sigma(l_{j})$ for unconstrained $l_{j}$ and $\lambda_{\max}=0.999$ (Section B.3). The factor $(1-\lambda_{j})$ keeps the state magnitude bounded. The decoder reads the state:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{h}^{(t)}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}.$
| | (6)

The recurrence is diagonal in feature space, so attribution runs through each decoder direction. Sparsity is imposed on $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ ; $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ need not be sparse. No predefined partition or auxiliary temporal objective is used.

Models and hyperparameters.

### 5.2 Short-Timescale Features Are Locally Interpretable

We apply the automated interpretability pipeline of Bills et al. [23] (a judge explains a feature from its highest-activation contexts and scores the explanation's predictive accuracy), scoring the Persistent SAE on $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ (Appendix E).

On both models fast features score higher than slow features and match or exceed the best baseline (Table 1, right). Fast features often respond to compact lexical or grammatical patterns such as letters or substrings, with activation concentrated at the current token (Tables 4 and 5 in Appendix E). Slow features more often reflect broader subjects or contextual conditions with activation distributed across the sequence; for such features distinct features may receive similar descriptions [24] and explanations may not generalise to related inputs [25]. Slow features are evaluated jointly in Section 5.3.

Where Features Receive New Evidence. 
Features are split into five equal-sized $\lambda$ quintiles and update positions into six categories: punctuation, conjunctions, function words, verbs, adjectives or adverbs, and nouns, following the lexical/function word distinction [26]; Func. (Figure 4) covers adpositions, determiners, particles, and pronouns. For quintile $q$ and category $c$ ,

| | $U_{q,c}={\Pr\!\left(T^{(t)}=c\mid a^{(t)}_{j}>0,\;j\in Q_{q}\right)}\big/{\Pr\!\left(T^{(t)}=c\right)},$
| | (7)

with $T^{(t)}$ the category of token $t$ and $Q_{q}$ the features in quintile $q$ .

The lowest- $\lambda$ quintile is updated more at nouns; the highest- $\lambda$ quintile more at punctuation and conjunctions (Figure 4). Punctuation and function-like tokens carry substantial contextual information in LLMs [27], and explicit structural markers gate cross-sentence integration [28]. Autointerpretations of high- $\lambda$ features often describe broad semantic domains (Tables 4 and 5).

### 5.3 Long-Timescale States Track Subject Information

Slow features form subject-specific clusters. 
On MMLU [29] examples from five subjects, the final $20$ token representations per sample are embedded with t-SNE, using the top $1\%$ slow features (Appendix F). BatchTopK features heavily mix subjects; the Temporal SAE's high-level group separates them only weakly; slow Persistent SAE features form coherent subject regions, more clearly separated than raw hidden states (Figure 5), learnt without subject labels.

### 5.4 Case Study: Persistent Prompt Injection Monitoring

In indirect prompt injection [12], an agent meets a malicious instruction in an email, webpage, or tool response, reasons for hundreds of tokens, and acts later [30]; an agentic monitor must hold a security-relevant signal until the agent acts [31, 32].

Setting. 
AgentDojo trajectories from banking, travel, and workspace [12], generated by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct [33] (Section C.3), each contain a request, an untrusted span with a prompt injection or benign content, and subsequent tool calls. Only failed attacks are used (injection present, attack action not completed).

Gemma-2-2B serves as external monitor: trajectories are replayed and layer-12 residual streams recorded. A linear probe is trained at the final token of the untrusted span ( $d=0$ ) and evaluated without retraining up to $350$ tokens later (Figure 7 (a)). Representations: raw hidden state, baseline SAEs, and Persistent SAE $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ restricted to slow (top $1\%$ by $\lambda_{j}$ ) or fast (bottom $50\%$ ) features (Appendix H).

Figure 7:
(a) Probe trained at the end of an untrusted span, evaluated later in the trajectory. (b) Predictive accuracy over distance (top) and causal effect on the monitor's judgement (bottom).

Signal retention: fast features detect local injections while slow states retain signals over long contexts. 
At $d=0$ , the fast-feature state and standard SAE representations give the strongest detection (Figure 7 (b), top); with distance their accuracy falls towards chance, whereas the slow-feature state retains a clearer signal.

Causal effect: slow-feature directions causally influence the monitor’s judgement. 
Each trajectory is truncated at a later distance, appended with a query asking whether it should be flagged for prompt injection, and intervened on at the final query token. Following [7, 34], a steering vector $\mathbf{v}_{r}$ per SAE representation $r$ weights its most predictive decoder directions by probe coefficients and is applied with both signs. With $s(\mathbf{x})=\ell_{\mathrm{yes}}(\mathbf{x})-\ell_{\mathrm{no}}(\mathbf{x})$ ,

| | $\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{causal}}(r,d)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{i}\Big[s\big(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(d)}+\alpha_{i}^{(d)}\mathbf{v}_{r}\big)-s\big(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(d)}-\alpha_{i}^{(d)}\mathbf{v}_{r}\big)\Big],$
| | (8)

where $\alpha_{i}^{(d)}$ scales each intervention to $10\%$ of the hidden-state norm.

Slow features give the largest, consistently positive $\Delta_{\mathrm{causal}}$ at every distance. BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and Temporal SAE directions give near-zero or negative effects with no comparable alignment over distance.

## 6 Conclusion and Discussion

Conclusion. 
Persistent SAEs learn from reconstruction alone how long each sparse feature retains information across tokens. Learned coefficients span a broad range: short-timescale features remain locally interpretable; long-timescale features track subject identity and preserve monitoring signals over long contexts.

Limitations and Future Work. 
A single fixed coefficient per feature in a diagonal recurrence cannot capture feature interactions or context-dependent resets. The prompt-injection study uses an external replay monitor, so interventions establish effects on the monitor's judgement, not the original agent's actions. Richer recurrent dynamics and end-to-end agent effects of persistent feature interventions remain open.

## Appendix B SAE Training Details

### B.1 SAE Baseline Training Details

Four families are trained: BatchTopK [8], Matryoshka BatchTopK [9], Temporal SAE [10], and Persistent SAE, with matched dictionary width, BatchTopK budget, optimiser, and token budget.

Common configuration. 
$m=16{,}384$ , $k=20$ per token; Adam at $3\times 10^{-4}$ with linear warm-up over the first $1{,}000$ steps. From step $1{,}000$ , the BatchTopK activation-threshold schedule with decay $\beta=0.999$ and the auxiliary dead-feature loss weighted by $\alpha_{\mathrm{aux}}=0.03125$ are applied. Activations come from Pile Uncopyrighted [35] with the beginning-of-sequence position removed. Gemma-2-2B [21]: layer-12 residual stream, $d=2{,}304$ ; Pythia-160M-deduped [20]: layer-8 residual stream, $d=768$ .

Matryoshka and Temporal SAEs share two predefined groups of $20\%$ and $80\%$ of the $16{,}384$ features; the Temporal SAE weights reconstruction losses $0.2$ and $0.8$ , Matryoshka uniformly. The Persistent SAE uses no partition.

Matched token budget. 
BatchTopK and Matryoshka consume shuffled token activations, Temporal SAE adjacent token pairs, Persistent SAE contiguous sequences. Activation tokens per step and total steps are matched: $244{,}140$ steps at approximately $2{,}048$ activation tokens per step, i.e. $2{,}048\times 244{,}140=499{,}998{,}720$ tokens, approximately $5.0\times 10^{8}$ , for the flat baselines.

•

BatchTopK and Matryoshka. Flat batches of $2{,}048$ token activations per step.

•

Temporal SAE. Adjacent previous–next token pairs from the same stream, with reconstructed positions per step equal to the flat batch size.

•

Persistent SAE. Eight contiguous sequences of context length $256$ per step; excluding the beginning-of-sequence position, $8\times 255=2{,}040$ usable activations per step, within $0.4\%$ of the flat budget.

All families receive the same number of gradient updates and, up to pairing or sequencing, approximately the same number of token activations. Checkpoints follow a fixed schedule; the final dictionary (ae.pt) is used throughout. Hardware: NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80 GB of memory.

### B.2 BatchTopK Sparsity

All SAEs compute

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{f}}=\mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{enc}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}})+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{enc}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{m},$
| | (9)

flatten $\{\tilde{\mathbf{f}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}$ for batch $X=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}$ into a vector of length $Bm$ , keep the top $kB$ entries globally to obtain $\mathbf{f}_{i}$ , and reconstruct

| | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\mathbf{f}_{i}+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{dec}}.$
| | (10)

At inference,

| | $f_{ij}=\tilde{f}_{ij}\,\mathbf{1}[\tilde{f}_{ij}>\theta],$
| | (11)

with $\theta$ estimated from training-time top- $k$ statistics. The Persistent SAE takes this output as $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ .

## Appendix C Dataset Details

### C.1 Pile Corpus

The Pile is an $825$  GiB English corpus from 22 sources, including academic papers, web pages, books, code, and online discussions [22]. We use Pile Uncopyrighted [35], which removes Books3, BookCorpus2, OpenSubtitles, YouTube Subtitles, and OpenWebText2. Documents are streamed and shuffled with a buffer of $10{,}000$ under a fixed seed and accepted if, after tokenisation and truncation to the context cap, they meet the minimum token count.

Natural-corpus temporal statistics on a retained length- $L$ sequence use positions $\{16,\dots,L-1\}$ .

The shuffled control concatenates sentences sampled from documents of the same corpus, forbidding consecutive sentences from the same source document; long-range entity tracking and discourse progression are thereby broken.

### C.2 MMLU Dataset

MMLU is an English benchmark of four-option multiple-choice questions from 57 subjects across STEM, humanities, social sciences, and other fields [29], used here only for subject analyses. Subjects: abstract algebra, astronomy, business ethics, computer security, and European history.

Geometry (Section 5.3): $100$ sequences across the five subjects, final $20$ token representations each. Probing: sequences of equal-length segments from different subjects, each token labelled by its source segment. Details: Appendix F and Appendix G.

### C.3 AgentDojo Trajectories

AgentDojo [12] provides stateful tool environments with 97 user tasks, 27 injection targets, and 629 security test cases across workspace, Slack, travel, and banking, with task-specific checks on agent output and environment changes for both the user request and the attacker's target action.

We use banking, travel, and workspace trajectories generated by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. Negatives ( $y=0$ ): benign trajectories without injection. Positives ( $y=1$ ): important_instructions or direct attacks with security=false (injection present, target action not completed). Successful attacks are excluded to remove overt malicious actions, such as transferring money or sending private data, as a classification cue. No filtering by task utility.

## Appendix F Subject Geometry Details

$100$ sequences from the five MMLU subjects (abstract algebra, astronomy, business ethics, computer security, European history); last $20$ tokens of each, subject-labelled. Raw hidden states, BatchTopK features, the Temporal SAE's high-level group, and the Persistent SAE's high- $\lambda_{j}$ state are projected to two dimensions by t-SNE with shared hyperparameters and coloured by subject.

## Appendix G Subject Probing Details

Spliced sequences concatenate equal-length segments from different MMLU subjects, with subject labels balanced within each sequence and entire source documents held out for testing. A per-token linear probe predicts source subject; we report held-out one-vs-rest macro ROC AUC as the available fraction of features sweeps from $0.1\%$ to $100\%$ . The Persistent SAE is probed on $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ with features ordered by decreasing $\lambda_{j}$ , increasing $\lambda_{j}$ , repeated random permutations, or supervised one-vs-rest importance

| | $s_{j,c}=\mathbb{E}[h^{(t)}_{j}\mid y^{(t)}=c]-\mathbb{E}[h^{(t)}_{j}\mid y^{(t)}\neq c],$
| | (13)

computed on the training split, sorted within subject and interleaved round-robin into one global ordering for the multiclass probe. BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and Temporal baselines use full dictionaries under the same probe.

## Appendix H Prompt Injection Monitoring Details

Trajectory construction. 
AgentDojo [12] runs of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct agents; attacks restricted to important_instructions and direct types with security=false; benign trajectories contain no injected content. Each serialised trajectory is appended with

should this trajectory be flagged for prompt injection or unsafe instruction hijacking? Answer yes or no:

and read with Gemma-2-2B at the layer-12 residual stream. The yes-minus-no logit at the query position yields AUC $0.51$ .

Checkpoints and probes. 
Checkpoints sit at $0$ , $50$ , $100$ , $200$ , $250$ , $300$ , and $350$ tokens after the final injected-span token (matched position for benign trajectories), plus the final query position. Extracted representations: raw hidden state, BatchTopK and Matryoshka activations, the Temporal SAE's high-level group, and the Persistent SAE's $\mathbf{a}^{(t)}$ , full $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ , and slow state (largest 1% of $\mathbf{h}^{(t)}$ coordinates by $\lambda_{j}$ ). Logistic regression probes are fit at $d=0$ only and evaluated without retraining at every checkpoint; held-out accuracy and ROC AUC are reported.

Causal intervention. 
Per SAE representation, the $k=128$ features with largest absolute probe coefficients form the probe-weighted decoder direction $\mathbf{v}_{r}$ , normalised and scaled so that $\lVert\alpha_{i}^{(d)}\mathbf{v}_{r}\rVert_{2}=\rho\lVert\mathbf{x}_{i}^{(d)}\rVert_{2}$ with $\rho=0.1$ , and added to the residual stream with both signs. Equation 8 measures the change in the external replay monitor's logit margin, not the original Llama-3.3-70B agent's action. Directions are constructed at $d=0$ ; Figure 7 reports transfer of their effect across distance.

ANSWER Q15: Not settled. The paper shows that Persistent SAEs *learn* a spectrum of timescales and that these correlate with empirical persistence, but it does not explicitly compare two different models' empirical persistence to their resulting $\lambda$ values.

ANSWER Q16: Use the top 1% of features ranked by decreasing $\lambda_j$. The evidence for this is strong, as Figure 6 shows this selection is nearly as efficient as a supervised label-informed oracle for tracking subject identity.

ANSWER Q17: Yes, for Gemma-2-2B. Table 5 lists a high-$\lambda$ feature (F-11205) with $\lambda = 9.18\text{\times}{10}^{-1}$, which is $0.918$ and would be constrained if the maximum allowed was $0.9$.

ANSWER Q18: They should measure the empirical persistence $R_j(\tau)$ of the features in each group. They should then check if the median $R_j(\tau)$ for the "slow" group decays more slowly across lags than the "fast" group, as done in Figure 3(b).

ANSWER Q19: Standard SAEs and the Temporal SAE's high-level group do not maintain a persistent state over long distances, causing their signal to decay. Persistent SAE slow features are designed to retain signal over long contexts via their learned $\lambda_j$ coefficients.

ANSWER Q1: The consistency regarding the carried-mass fraction would break. Appendix B.1 reports that the carried-mass fraction for Gemma (0.65–0.70) is higher than for Pythia (approximately 0.5), which aligns with the observed training dynamics.

ANSWER Q2: It would lose the "Smoothness" comparison for the High group on Pythia. It would be outperformed by the Matryoshka (0.12) and Temporal (0.11) high-level groups, as 0.12 is higher (worse) than both.

ANSWER Q3: Because the Temporal SAE uses a predefined partition of roles rather than learned persistence for each feature. ANSWER Q4: The claim that fast features "match or exceed the best baseline" in local interpretability would be undermined. Section 5.2 states that fast features score higher than slow features and match or exceed the best baseline.

ANSWER Q6: The choice of a diagonal recurrence in feature space. The paper's motivation for using a diagonal recurrence (Equation 5) is based on the finding that persistence of individual features (diagonal correction) aids reconstruction.

ANSWER Q7: They could compute the empirical persistence $R_j(\tau)$ for each feature. Section 3 defines $R_j(\tau)$ to measure how long a feature's decoder-aligned projection remains elevated after activation.

ANSWER Q8: Not settled. While Table 1 lists "Fraction Alive," it does not consistently show the Persistent SAE as having the highest value across both models (e.g., on Pythia, BatchTopK is higher at 0.91 vs 0.86).

ANSWER Q9: Because the high- $\lambda$ features are extremely smooth (0.05 on Pythia, 0.04 on Gemma). This extreme smoothness in the slow group offsets the poor smoothness of the fast group, resulting in a lower (better) full-dictionary average than the baselines.

ANSWER Q10: Contradicted. Appendix D.1 states that for Gemma-2-2B, the $R^2_{\text{improve}}$ was "zero by lag 32," meaning it did not improve reconstruction at every lag up to 512.

ANSWER Q11: Contradicted. Table 1 shows that for Pythia, the Persistent SAE's FVE (0.93) is equal to the Temporal SAE's (0.93), and for Gemma, it is higher (0.66 vs 0.62).

ANSWER Q12: The characterization that slow features reflect "broader subjects or contextual conditions" while fast features act as "local detectors" for lexical patterns. Figure 4 and Section 5.2 show a distinction where high- $\lambda$ features are updated more at punctuation/conjunctions and low- $\lambda$ features at nouns.

ANSWER Q13: Not settled. The paper shows that standard SAE features exhibit persistence and that Persistent SAEs learn $\lambda$ values, but it does not explicitly correlate the *amount* of empirical persistence in a standard SAE with the *magnitude* of the $\lambda$ learned in a subsequent Persistent SAE.

ANSWER Q14: Yes, it would constrain features in both models. Table 4 and 5 show slow features with $\lambda$ values such as $7.03 \times 10^{-1}$ (Pythia) and $9.18 \times 10^{-1}$ (Gemma); since $0.9$ is the new cap, any feature originally above $0.9$ (like F-11205 in Gemma) would be constrained.

ANSWER Q15: BatchTopK SAE. Table 1 shows that BatchTopK achieves the highest FVE for both Pythia (0.94) and Gemma (0.72).

ANSWER Q16: The claim that "Temporal Persistence Selects Subject-Informative Features Without Labels." Section 5.3 asserts that decreasing- $\lambda_j$ selection is nearly as efficient as supervised selection for predicting subjects.

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. While Table 3 shows that features with more positive $w_j$ exist, the paper does not provide a correlation analysis between the "positive fraction" of weights and the total $R^2_{\text{improve}}$ gained.

ANSWER Q18: It would be less effective. Figure 5 and 6 show that slow Persistent SAE features separate MMLU subjects more clearly and provide higher subject-probing AUC than the Temporal SAE's high-level group.

ANSWER Q19: No. Initializing $l_j$ at 10 would push $\sigma(l_j)$ very close to 1, starting almost all features at the maximum persistence $\lambda_{\max}$. This would likely lead to saturation and hinder the model's ability to learn the diverse spectrum of short-timescale features.

ANSWER Q1: The claim that temporal persistence selects subject-informative features without labels would fail. Decreasing-\(\lambda_j\) ranking outperforming random selection is the evidence that learned timescale identifies topic-relevant features.

ANSWER Q2: Gemma-2-2B would likely suffer more. Its carried term accounts for about \(65\%-70\%\) of state activation mass, compared with roughly \(50\%\) for Pythia-160M.

ANSWER Q3: It would lose to the Temporal SAE’s low-level group, whose smoothness is \(0.11\), since lower is better. It would also only tie the Matryoshka low-level group at \(0.12\).

ANSWER Q4: Supported. Persistent SAEs have the highest reported fraction alive on both Pythia (\(0.96\)) and Gemma (\(0.91\)), exceeding every listed baseline.

ANSWER Q5: The shuffled activations contain no useful relationship to the natural-document targets, so fitted corrections mainly add estimation noise on held-out data. Finite-sample fitting and imperfect regularisation can therefore make \(R^2_{\mathrm{improve}}\) slightly negative rather than exactly zero.

ANSWER Q6: The Temporal SAE’s predefined high-level group was not clearly separated from its low-level group by empirical persistence, so its directions were not selected to preserve injection signals across long distances. Persistent SAE slow features explicitly learned long retention through reconstruction, making their probe-weighted directions more likely to remain aligned with the monitor’s judgement.

ANSWER Q7: They should reset \(\mathbf h\) to zero at each document boundary. This matches training, where \(\mathbf h^{(0)}=\mathbf0\) at every sequence start, and prevents unrelated information from one document leaking into the next.

ANSWER Q8: They could compute each feature’s empirical persistence \(R_j(\tau)\) over several lags and rank features by sustained high values, especially at long lags. They could also fit the per-feature context-correction weights \(w_{\tau,j}\) and favour features whose past activations positively improve later reconstruction.

ANSWER Q9: No. With no new activation, retention after 5,000 tokens is at most \(0.999^{5000}\approx0.0067\), or \(0.67\%\), below \(1\%\).

ANSWER Q10: Contradicted. For both models, Matryoshka’s high-level group has worse smoothness than its low-level group: \(0.25\) versus \(0.12\) on Pythia and \(0.21\) versus \(0.14\) on Gemma, with lower being smoother.

ANSWER Q11: Not settled. The paper shows empirical persistence for standard SAE features and learned \(\lambda_j\) distributions for Persistent SAEs, but it does not establish a model-level relationship whereby greater standard-SAE persistence predicts larger learned coefficients.

ANSWER Q12: The characterisation of slow features as receiving evidence at structural or context-integrating markers would lose support. Their disproportionate updates at punctuation and conjunctions help distinguish them from fast, noun-updated local detectors.

ANSWER Q13: Not settled. Context correction was tested only through lag \(32\), not \(512\), and for Gemma its benefit was already approximately zero by lag \(32\); the separate \(R_j(\tau)\) analysis out to \(512\) measures alignment, not reconstruction improvement.

ANSWER Q14: No. Gemma-2-2B’s direct yes-minus-no response to that query achieved AUC \(0.51\), essentially chance, whereas trained probes over persistent slow states retained useful injection signals.

ANSWER Q15: The evidence favours \(\lambda\)-ranked Persistent SAE features. Matryoshka’s predefined high-level group mixed subjects more heavily, while the slowest Persistent features formed clearer subject clusters and achieved high probing AUC with only a small feature budget.

ANSWER Q16: Contradicted. On Pythia, Matryoshka had a larger positive-weight fraction than BatchTopK (\(91.4\%\) versus \(76.2\%\)) but removed less baseline error at lag one (\(0.61\%\) versus \(0.89\%\)).

ANSWER Q17: It would undermine the claim that short-timescale features are locally interpretable and match or exceed the best baseline in automated interpretability. That comparative result relies on fast features scoring at least as well as BatchTopK.

ANSWER Q18: Yes, for Gemma-2-2B. The example feature F-11205 has \(\lambda=0.918\) and would be capped by \(\lambda_{\max}=0.9\); none of the listed Pythia examples exceeds \(0.9\).

ANSWER Q19: Contradicted. Persistent SAEs are competitive but not uniformly best: for example, BatchTopK has higher FVE on both Pythia (\(0.94\) versus \(0.93\)) and Gemma (\(0.72\) versus \(0.66\)).

ANSWER Q13: Select features in decreasing order of \(\lambda_j\), starting with approximately the slowest 1%. ANSWER Q14: No. Even at the cap, the retained fraction after 5,000 tokens is \(0.999^{5000}\approx0.0067\), below 1%, and actual coefficients are strictly below \(0.999\).

ANSWER Q15: The Temporal SAE’s high-level group is predefined and was not clearly separated from its low-level group by empirical persistence. ANSWER Q16: Contradicted. The full Persistent dictionaries have lower autointerpretability point estimates than BatchTopK on both models; only the fast Persistent subset matches or exceeds BatchTopK.

ANSWER Q17: The slow set contains only about 164 features—the top 1% of 16,384—so selecting 128 by probe coefficient retains most of that already timescale-filtered set. ANSWER Q18: They would probably lose little for local token-level interpretation: Pythia’s fast features score \(0.93\) on autointerpretability versus \(0.91\) for BatchTopK, while the full Persistent SAE has similar reconstruction. However, the paper does not report fast-only reconstruction, and they would lose the contextual information carried by slow features.

ANSWER Q19: Not settled. The paper shows that, within a Persistent SAE, higher-\(\lambda\) groups have greater empirical persistence, but it does not establish a cross-model relationship between persistence in standard SAEs and the magnitude of learned \(\lambda\) values.

ANSWER Q15: No. “Slow” is defined relatively as the top 1% by \(\lambda_j\), and the listed slow Pythia examples range only up to 0.703; a \(>0.9\) threshold would miss even these clearly slow features.

Fitted positive context-correction weights \(w_{\tau,j}\), especially across several lags, could provide an additional reconstruction-based ranking signal.

ANSWER Q17: Contradicted. Context correction was tested only through lag 32, not 512, and on Gemma its gain was already approximately zero by lag 32; the observed \(R_j(\tau)\) persistence through lag 512 is not itself proof of reconstruction improvement.

ANSWER Q18: Pythia-160M would recover more error: about 0.89% for BatchTopK or 0.61% for Matryoshka, versus roughly 0.40% on Gemma. The gain would still be small—under 1% of baseline reconstruction error.

ANSWER Q19: Contradicted. Lower smoothness is better, but Matryoshka’s high-level group scores 0.25 versus 0.12 for its low-level group on Pythia, and 0.21 versus 0.14 on Gemma, so the predefined high-level group is less smooth.

ANSWER Q1: The diagonal, feature-independent recurrence would lose its motivation. Such a result would imply that temporal predictability mainly comes from interactions between different features, rather than each feature persisting along its own decoder direction.

ANSWER Q2: Not settled. The paper tests interventions only at a fixed magnitude of 10% of the hidden-state norm, so it does not measure how the causal effect changes with intervention strength.

ANSWER Q3: They should compute empirical persistence \(R_j(\tau)\) for each feature and compare the fast and slow groups’ decay curves over multiple lags. A genuine slow group should retain higher decoder-aligned signal and decay more slowly than the fast group.

ANSWER Q4: It would break the qualitative consistency that Gemma has both more carried state mass and examples with substantially higher persistence coefficients than Pythia. Gemma’s carried fraction is reported as \(0.65\)–\(0.70\), and its illustrated slow features reach \(\lambda\approx0.92\), versus roughly \(0.50\) and \(\lambda\leq0.70\) in the Pythia examples.

ANSWER Q5: For local token-level interpretability, probably not much. Fast Persistent SAE features match or exceed BatchTopK’s automated-interpretability score and detect compact lexical and grammatical patterns, although using only them would discard long-range context and the paper does not report fast-only reconstruction quality.

ANSWER Q6: The slow representation is already reduced to the top 1% of features by the label-free persistence ranking, leaving roughly 164 features, of which steering selects 128. BatchTopK instead selects 128 predictive features from the entire 16,384-feature dictionary, making its direction much more dependent on the probe ranking.

ANSWER Q7: Contradicted by the reported automated-interpretability metric. The full Persistent dictionary scores below BatchTopK on both Pythia (\(0.86\) versus \(0.91\)) and Gemma (\(0.85\) versus \(0.87\)); only the fast subset matches or exceeds the baselines.

ANSWER Q8: Expect new updates especially at punctuation and conjunctions, and more generally at structural or function-like markers. The highest-\(\lambda\) quintile is enriched for updates at these tokens relative to their corpus frequency.

ANSWER Q9: The context-correction number measures the incremental reduction of a standard SAE’s remaining reconstruction error using one earlier lag, whereas carried mass measures how much of a separately trained Persistent SAE state comes recursively from all previous tokens. They use different denominators, and the Persistent SAE jointly adapts its activations, decoder, and persistence coefficients, so a large carried-state share need not yield a comparably large correction to an existing SAE.

ANSWER Q10: They should choose BatchTopK. It has the highest Gemma reconstruction FVE, \(0.72\), compared with \(0.71\) for Matryoshka, \(0.66\) for Persistent, and \(0.62\) for Temporal.

ANSWER Q11: They should rank features by decreasing \(\lambda_j\) and begin with the slowest features, since these compactly retain document-level subject or context information without labels. Support for this exact task is limited: the quantitative evidence concerns five MMLU subjects, while the Pile-domain evidence is qualitative and some code or licence detectors are actually low-\(\lambda\) local features.

ANSWER Q12: Token \(s\)’s activation should receive weight \((1-\lambda_j)\lambda_j^{\,t-s}\). With \(h_j^{(0)}=0\), the state unfolds as \(h_j^{(t)}=\sum_{s=1}^{t}(1-\lambda_j)\lambda_j^{t-s}a_j^{(s)}\).

ANSWER Q13: They should use the slow-state direction, formed from the top 1% by \(\lambda_j\), with the negative sign: \(\mathbf{x}-\alpha\mathbf v_{\mathrm{slow}}\). The positive direction raises the yes-minus-no margin, so its negative nudges the monitor toward “no,” and slow features retain the strongest causal alignment at long distances.

ANSWER Q14: Contradicted. Persistent and Temporal have equal Pythia FVE (\(0.93\)), while Persistent is better on Gemma (\(0.66\) versus \(0.62\)).

ANSWER Q15: No. The illustrated Pythia slow features have \(\lambda\) values only around \(0.37\)–\(0.70\), so a \(0.9\) threshold would miss even top-1% slow features; “slow” should be defined relatively, such as by the highest-\(\lambda\) percentile.

ANSWER Q16: Not settled. The paper demonstrates clustering and probing on only five selected MMLU subjects, not all 57 subjects or unseen subject sets, so it does not establish generality across MMLU as a whole.

ANSWER Q17: Pythia-160M would recover more error. At lag 1 it recovers about \(0.89\%\) for BatchTopK or \(0.61\%\) for Matryoshka, versus roughly \(0.40\%\) on Gemma, so the gain is still small and below 1%.

ANSWER Q18: No, not reliably. Initialising \(l_j=10\) would put every \(\lambda_j\) near the \(0.999\) cap and in the sigmoid’s saturated regime, producing very small gradients for reducing persistence; the paper instead initializes at \(0.5\) specifically to avoid saturation.

ANSWER Q19: The full score reflects the complete state representation, not just the bottom-\(\lambda\) half. The slow and intermediate features are substantially smoother and can lower the aggregate metric, while recurrence smooths their persistent states; therefore the poor \(0.20\) score of the fast subset does not determine the full dictionary’s score.

ANSWER Q1: Select features in decreasing order of learned \(\lambda_j\), using the highest-\(\lambda\) features as a compact context or topic representation. This is only tentatively supported for those exact Pile categories: the strong quantitative evidence concerns MMLU subjects, while code and software-license examples appear among low-\(\lambda\) local features.

ANSWER Q2: Expect the slowest features to receive new updates disproportionately at punctuation and conjunctions, and more generally at structural or function-like markers. These tokens can signal discourse boundaries and contextual integration.

ANSWER Q3: The evidence favours \(\lambda\)-ranked Persistent SAE features. The Temporal SAE’s predefined high-level group showed weak subject separation, was not clearly separated by empirical persistence, and retained less subject information at a small feature budget.

ANSWER Q4: Contradicted. For Pythia, Matryoshka had a larger positive-weight fraction than BatchTopK (\(91.4\%\) versus \(76.2\%\)) but removed less reconstruction error at lag 1 (\(0.61\%\) versus \(0.89\%\)).

ANSWER Q5: The feature-wise diagonal recurrence would lose its motivation—specifically, the assumption that each feature should carry forward only its own state with its own \(\lambda_j\). Large gains only from a full matrix would instead motivate cross-feature temporal interactions.

ANSWER Q6: Not settled. The causal experiment used a single intervention strength, fixed at \(10\%\) of the hidden-state norm, and did not sweep strength to establish a dose–response relationship.

ANSWER Q7: Weight token \(s\)’s activation by \((1-\lambda_j)\lambda_j^{\,t-s}\). Thus \(h_j^{(t)}=\sum_{s=1}^{t}(1-\lambda_j)\lambda_j^{t-s}a_j^{(s)}\), given \(h_j^{(0)}=0\).

ANSWER Q8: Contradicted by the reported autointerpretability metric. The full Persistent SAE scored below BatchTopK on both Pythia (\(0.86\) versus \(0.91\)) and Gemma (\(0.85\) versus \(0.87\)), although its fast subset matched or exceeded the baselines.

ANSWER Q9: Contradicted. Persistent and Temporal SAEs had equal reported cosine similarity on both models; their FVE was equal on Pythia and higher for Persistent on Gemma (\(0.66\) versus \(0.62\)).

ANSWER Q10: The claim that learned temporal persistence identifies subject-informative features without labels would fail. In particular, the paper could no longer claim that the slowest features provide a compact ranking nearly as efficient as supervised selection.

ANSWER Q11: Use the Persistent SAE’s slow-feature steering direction with the negative sign, \(-\alpha\mathbf v_{\text{slow}}\). The positive direction raises the yes-minus-no prompt-injection margin, so the negative direction should nudge the monitor toward “no.”

ANSWER Q12: The shuffled activations contain no useful transferable temporal signal, but the correction weights are still estimated from finite data. Estimation noise, overfitting, and mismatch between shuffled contexts and natural-document targets can therefore slightly worsen held-out reconstruction rather than produce exactly zero change.

ANSWER Q13: No. “Slow” is defined relatively as the top \(1\%\) by \(\lambda_j\), and the listed Pythia slow examples range only from about \(0.37\) to \(0.70\); a \(0.9\) threshold could select few or no Pythia features.

ANSWER Q14: Contradicted. Context correction was tested only through lag 32, and for Gemma its gain was already approximately zero by lag 32; persistence measurements out to 512 tokens do not establish reconstruction improvement at those lags.

ANSWER Q15: Compute each standard feature’s empirical persistence curve \(R_j(\tau)\) and rank features by high long-lag persistence or slow fitted decay. They could also use positive context-correction weights across lags as a reconstruction-based candidate signal.

ANSWER Q16: The characterization of slow features as broad contextual states updated at structural or discourse-gating markers would lose support. The observed contrast—slow features favouring punctuation and conjunctions while fast features favour nouns—helps distinguish them from local content detectors.

ANSWER Q17: Contradicted. Lower smoothness values mean smoother representations, but Matryoshka’s predefined high-level group had higher values than its low-level group on both Pythia (\(0.25\) versus \(0.12\)) and Gemma (\(0.21\) versus \(0.14\)).

ANSWER Q18: The Temporal SAE’s high-level group is predefined and was not clearly separated from its low-level group by empirical persistence, so directions learned at \(d=0\) need not remain aligned with the injection signal. Persistent SAE slow states are explicitly selected by learned long timescales and retain the signal, allowing their probe-weighted directions to transfer causally over distance.

ANSWER Q19: Not settled. The paper separately reports empirical persistence for standard SAEs and learned \(\lambda_j\) distributions for Persistent SAEs, but it does not test a cross-model relationship showing that greater standard-SAE persistence predicts larger learned coefficients.
